b.bio: Aristotle was an ancient Greek philosopher and polymath from Stagira who studied under Plato at the Academy in Athens. He subsequently founded the Lyceum and established the Peripatetic school of philosophy, authoring foundational treatises in logic, metaphysics, ethics, politics, and natural sciences. His core logical treatises, known collectively as the Organon, were translated into Latin by Boethius and others, leading to their inclusion in Latin theological corpora and establishing Aristotle as a cornerstone of medieval Christian scholastic theology.
b.s: Aristotle's logical writings established the standard apparatus of formal logic and dialectic that shaped Christian scholastic theology throughout the Middle Ages.

On the Breaking of the Body of Christ

b.bio: Abbo of Fleury, born near Orléans around 945, was a Benedictine monk educated at Paris and Reims in philosophy, mathematics, and astronomy. He spent two years in England directing the school at the newly founded monastery of Ramsey, then returned to Fleury and was elected abbot there in 988 after Abbot Oilbold's death, a contested choice settled in his favor by Gerbert of Aurillac. He took part in the Synod of St. Basle near Reims and died on 13 November 1004.
b.s: The tract held here defends that Christ's body is truly broken in the sacrament against those who denied it, arguing from the words of institution that eucharistic mysteries are to be believed rather than reasoned out by natural bodily laws.

b.bio: Abbo of Metz, also called Goericus or Goeric, was a Merovingian bishop of Metz who succeeded St. Arnulf in the see (sources give 627 or 629 for the succession) and died in 643; the New Catholic Encyclopedia gives 647 as an alternative death date. He was ordained a priest by Arnulf, transferred Arnulf's relics to the Church of the Apostles, built Great St. Peter's at Metz and a monastery at Epinal for his daughters Precia and Victorina, and was a personal friend of King Dagobert I, whose will calls him Abbo. The medieval Vita Goerici is judged wholly unreliable.
b.s: The library's single item under his name is an epistle from PL 87: among the letters of St. Desiderius of Cahors there is one letter to Abbo and one from him (PL 87:253, 262), making these epistles the surviving trace of his correspondence.

b.bio: Absalon (also called Axel) was born around 1128 in Seeland into the powerful Hvide clan and died on 21 March 1201 at Sorø Abbey, which his father had founded. Educated at Paris, he taught at Ste Geneviève before becoming Bishop of Roskilde in 1158 and Archbishop of Lund in 1178, serving as primate of Denmark and Sweden and eventually papal legate. As chief adviser to Valdemar I and Canute VI he led the campaign that captured the Wend stronghold of Rügen in 1169 and built the first fortification of the city that grew into Copenhagen. It was at his request that Saxo Grammaticus composed the Historiæ Danicæ.
b.s: The single work held here (PL 209) concerns his Testament: a deathbed disposition whose text raises questions the surrounding material argues over—whether it was oral rather than written, whether clerics exempt from Danish law could make testaments freely, and the chronology of his episcopal career.

b.bio: Achard was born around 1100, in England by one account, into the Norman family of de Pertins of Domfront by another. He completed his studies at the abbey school of Saint-Victor in Paris and entered its cloister. On the death of the first abbot, Gilduin, in 1155 he was elected second abbot of Saint-Victor, holding the post until 1161. In 1157 the cathedral chapter of Sées elected him bishop, and the choice was confirmed by Adrian IV, but Henry II intervened and intruded his own candidate; subsequent relations between Achard and the king were cordial, and Achard used his influence at court to compel the royal treasurer Richard of Ely to disburse money unjustly detained from the poor — a letter to Henry II on this matter survives. In 1162 he became Bishop of Avranches, with no objection from Henry II. Sources give his death as 1171 or 1172.
b.s: The letter held here shows him compelling restitution owed to churches and the poor, arguing that service to the least is service rendered to Christ and that neglect of debts to the poor brings judgment before God.

w: Poem to King Robert of France

b.bio: Adalbero, also called Ascelin, was bishop of Laon from 977 until his death; sources disagree on his date of death (19 July 1030/1031 in one account; a 27 January, probably 1031, per Arlima). Nephew of Adalbero, archbishop of Reims, he studied at Reims and served as chancellor to King Lothaire (974). His career was turbulent: accused by Richer of Rheims of adultery with Queen Emma, removed from Laon in 981, imprisoned when Charles of Lower Lorraine took the city in 988, restored, and finally in 991 delivering Laon, Charles, and Archbishop Arnulf into Hugh Capet's hands.
b.s: The work held here is his Carmen ad Rotbertum regem, a satirical dialogue poem dedicated to Robert II of France opposing contemporary episcopal and monastic reform, notably the Cluniac reforms and Odilo of Cluny, whom it attacks directly. Recent scholarship questions whether it is anti-Cluniac polemic or a commentary on monastic hypocrisy. The text as held here treats the heavenly Jerusalem, an earthly order patterned on the heavenly hierarchy, and true wisdom given by grace.

w: Introduction of monks into the monastery of Mouzon

b.bio: Adalbero of Reims, also called Adalbero of Ardennes, was archbishop of Reims and chancellor to Kings Lothair and Louis V of West Francia. A native of Lorraine, son of Count Gozlin of Bidgau and Methingau and Oda of Metz, he was named archbishop by Emperor Otto I and pursued an alliance with the Ottonian dynasty against Carolingian attempts to recover Lorraine. Accused of treason by Louis V, he escaped trial when the king died in 987; he then declared the Frankish crown elective and crowned Hugh Capet, excluding Duke Charles of Lower Lorraine. He died on 23 January 989.
b.s: The works held here are letters and a record on monastic transfer that show him governing his province amid the Lothair–Ottonian conflict: civil disorder devastating the churches, rendering to caesar and God each his due, holy orders conferring spiritual rather than temporal jurisdiction, and monks moved between houses by mutual consent.

b.bio: Adalbert of Metz compiled the Speculum Gregorii, a four-book selection of 193 excerpts from Gregory the Great's Moralia in Job, each given a heading of his own devising, dedicated to his friend Hermann. In the prologue he calls himself a deacon; in the epilogue, a monk and priest. His epitaph by Gerbert of Aurillac says he was noble-born and died young on 12 February, dated variously to 962 or about 980. Trithemius in the 16th century assigned him to Saint-Vincent de Metz. He is not to be confused with Adalbert of Spalding, a 12th-century Benedictine.
b.s: His Speculum Gregorii was one of the main medieval channels for Gregory's Moralia, copied widely (a French manuscript of about 970 was already at Christ Church Canterbury before the end of that century) and listed in many English monastic catalogues; the library holds its prologue, addressed to Hermann, defending the humble 'mirror' against envious critics.

b.bio: Adalbert I von Saarbrücken, of the family of the Counts of Saarbrücken, served as imperial chancellor under Henry IV and Henry V before being named Archbishop of Mainz in 1111 as reward for his part in the embassy that produced the Treaty of Sutri and Henry V's coronation. Once invested, he turned against the Emperor: Henry imprisoned him without trial from 1112 to 1115 for refusing to surrender control of imperial castles, and after his release Adalbert fomented unrest in the upper Rhineland and backed Lothair III's election in 1125 over Henry's chosen heir. The letters held here concern episcopal consecration, the restoration of repentant bishops, the role of legates, concord between bishop and canons, and grace perfecting repentance; they argue against the clergy of Halberstadt.
b.s: His letters are evidence of Gregorian positions on investiture and episcopal discipline from the archbishop who did most to defeat Henry V's design on the German church.

w: Homily on the Feast of St. Alexius the Confessor
Profession of the Rule of Saint Benedict

b.bio: Adalbert (Vojtěch), born c. 956 at Libice nad Cidlinou into the Slavník princely family of Bohemia, studied theology at Magdeburg and became the first bishop of Prague of Czech origin. He worked as a missionary among the Hungarians, Poles, and Baltic Prussians, and was martyred on 23 April 997 while converting the Prussians; he was canonized in 999 by Pope Sylvester II. The library holds under his name a homily for the feast of Alexius the Confessor and a profession of the Rule of Saint Benedict, both printed in PL 137.
b.s: The two short pieces held here — a homily on Alexius asserting renunciation of all things for discipleship, patient endurance enabled by divine love, and the hundredfold reward, and a Benedictine profession treating monastic obedience as imitation of the saint — are devotional texts associated with his cult rather than major theological works.

b.bio: Adalard, son of Bernard (son of Charles Martel) and cousin of Charlemagne, was educated at the Palatine School and made Count of the Palace while still young. At about twenty he entered the monastery of Corbie in Picardy; he later withdrew to Monte Cassino, but was recalled by Charlemagne and elected abbot of Corbie, also serving as prime minister to Pepin, King of Italy. Banished to Noirmoutier under Louis the Pious after Bernard of Italy's bid for the imperial crown, he was restored after seven years as one of Louis's chief advisers, and in 822 founded New Corvey in Westphalia with his brother Wala.
b.s: The statutes held here are an early Carolingian monastic customary: rules on the fixed number of provisioners maintained by replacement, oversight of bell-ringers to protect the monastery's reputation, feast-day alms and rest for servants, and generous provision governed by need rather than human parsimony — practical legislation built on the Rule that shaped how Benedictine houses were administered.

w: History of the Archbishops of Hamburg

b.bio: Adam of Bremen, German historian and geographer of the eleventh century, was born before 1050 and died 12 October 1081 or 1085; the Catholic Encyclopedia notes that his exact birth and death dates are unknown. He came from Eastern Franconia or Western Thuringia, perhaps Bamberg or Würzburg; whether he studied at the Bamberg cathedral school cannot be assured. Archbishop Adalbert brought him to Bremen in 1066/1067 (the Catholic Encyclopedia says 1068), made him a canon and magister scholarum — his name appears on a charter of 11 June 1069 as Adam magister scolarum. He signed his preface only 'A.', the name Adam being known through Helmold of Bosau's Chronica Slavorum.
b.s: His Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum is the chief source for the history and ethnography of the North before the thirteenth century; the library holds it in PL 146.

b.bio: Adefonsus Hispaniae is the name under which the library holds a single Latin letter (PL 151) on the promotion of Peter of Cardenas. The name corresponds to one of several medieval kings of Spain called Alfonso, and the printed form does not by itself identify which. The letter's citation of Pope Paschal places its business in a pontificate of a pope named Paschal; it also names Cardinal Regnerius, Didacus (Diego) II, bishop of Compostela, and King Alfonso. It is written as a history and argues that promotion to ecclesiastical office without Roman consent warrants canonical deposition. Sources describing other works under similar names — the anonymous Chronica Adefonsi Imperatoris on Alfonso VII, or the disputed Epistola Adefonsi Hispaniae regis of 906 — concern different texts and are not evidence for this letter.
b.s: The single work here is an early twelfth-century royal-ecclesiastical letter asserting that episcopal promotion without papal consent justifies canonical deposition.

On the Method of Finding the Thickness of a Sphere

b.bio: Adelbold of Utrecht (also printed Adalbold II) was born around the end of the tenth century, probably in the Low Countries, of a noble family in the diocese of Liège, and was educated there and at Rheims, partly under Notker of Liège. He became a canon of Laubach, was invited to the court of Emperor Henry II, who admitted him to his council and in 1010 made him bishop of Utrecht. He defended the see against Norman raids and neighboring nobles, lost the Merwede dispute against Dirk III of Holland at Vlaardingen (1018), and acquired the counties of Drente and Teisterbant in 1024 and 1026. Sources give his death as 27 November 1026 or 1027.
b.s: The works held here are his life of Emperor Henry II with its preface on the qualifications of an historian, his Life of St. Walpurga, and short treatises on music and on finding the thickness of a sphere.

b.bio: Adelgorius of Magdeburg — also printed as Adalgoz, Adelgot, or Adalgotus — was archbishop of Magdeburg who died in 1119. The letter held here, the Epistola ad Episcopos (PL 157, cols. 483–486D), is dated by Migne to 1100–1110 and is possibly his work: the CERL authority record notes that either Adalgotus or an anonymous Flemish cleric may be its author. The letter responds to pagan attacks on Christians, urging bishops toward holy war.
b.s: The single work here is a crusading appeal written after pagans profaned churches and slaughtered Christians, arguing that war against Christ's enemies is a religious duty that saves souls and that contemplatives must take up active service in time of need.

w: Letter on the Sacrament of the Eucharist
On Illustrious Men of His Time

b.bio: Adelmann, of unknown parentage and nationality, studied at Chartres under Fulbert alongside Berengarius of Tours, and became bishop of Brescia around 1050. He took part in the church-reform movement against simony and clerical concubinage. The library holds his letter to Berengarius on the Eucharist — a defense of the real presence addressed with evident affection to a former friend turned opponent — and the work printed as On Illustrious Men of His Time, which praises Fulbert's school and identifies Adelmann as prefect of the Liège schools.
b.s: His Eucharist letter is a primary witness to eleventh-century sacramental teaching against Berengarius, arguing that the eucharist is the true body and blood of Christ and that patristic consensus binds in faith.

b.bio: Adrianus III was bishop of Rome from 17 May 884 until his death on 8 July 885 near Modena, while traveling to the diet summoned by Charles the Fat to settle the imperial succession. Born in Rome, he succeeded Marinus I and was succeeded by Stephen V. His brief pontificate fell in a time of famine and war in Italy; he aided the Roman population during the famine and sent Theodosius of Brindisi and Oria to Constantinople with a synodal letter on faith and the filioque. He was buried at Nonantula, venerated locally, and canonized by Leo XIII in 1891.
b.s: The two texts held here are curial documents—a privilege and an epistle—asserting papal protection of monastic donations, the metropolitan's role in consecrating an abbess at a founder's summons, and the binding force of predecessors' privileges on papal successors, written against Girbert, bishop of Nîmes, and the party of Piacenza.

w: On the Miracles of St. Waldebert
On the Translation and Miracles of St. Basolus

b.bio: Adso Dervensis was a Benedictine monk of noble birth, educated at Luxeuil and a schoolmaster at Saint-Evre in Toul before becoming abbot of Montier-en-Der around 960/968. He knew Gerbert of Aurillac (later Pope Sylvester II), Abbo of Fleury, and Queen Gerberga, wife of Louis IV, to whom he addressed his tract on the Antichrist. He died in 992 while on pilgrimage to the Holy Land (one source reports he died at sea and was buried in the Cyclades). The library holds his De Antichristo (printed among Alcuin's works in PL 101) and six hagiographical works from PL 137: lives of Mansuetus, Bercharius, Frodobert, Basolus, and Waldebert, plus an account of the translation and miracles of St. Basolus.
b.s: His letter on the Antichrist became one of the most copied medieval descriptions of Antichrist and shaped all later apocalyptic tradition; the saints' lives here document the cults of Luxeuil- and Toul-region saints.

b.bio: Adventius was bishop of Metz from 855 until his death in 875, educated under his predecessor Drogo, son of Charlemagne. He served at the courts of Lothar II and Charles the Bald and spoke at the Synod of Metz in 869 and the Synod of Douzy in 871. He supported Lothar II's attempt to set aside Queen Theutberga in favor of Waldrada, composing a writing in favor of the divorce; the library's 'Booklet on Waldrada' belongs to this affair. His letters to Pope Nicholas I and to Archbishop Theutgaud of Trier concern the condemned metropolitans Gunthar of Cologne and Theutgaud himself.
b.s: His works here document the episcopal side of the Lothar II divorce crisis and the defense of papal authority over deposed metropolitans: deposed bishops may not minister, communion with the excommunicated must be shunned, and the pope holds God's place on earth.

b.bio: Ælfric was a monk of Abingdon, abbot of St Albans, and bishop of Ramsbury before his election to Canterbury on Easter Day 995; he was installed in 996 and received his pallium from Gregory V in Rome in 997. He is credited, possibly together with his predecessor Sigeric, with replacing the secular clergy of Canterbury Cathedral with monks. His will survives. The work held here is a pastoral-canonical instruction addressed to a bishop named Wulfin, treating clerical discipline: bishops must exemplify virtue and admonish rather than stay silent ('dumb dogs'), priests must fulfill their duties without negligence and must not hold secular offices such as sheriff, reeve, or bailiff, clergy must live without women in their households (against clerical marriage), and Constantine summoned Nicaea to confirm the catholic faith against Arius.
b.s: The Canons to Wulfin are a window into late Anglo-Saxon clerical reform, enforcing celibacy, residence, and the separation of priesthood from secular office.

b.bio: The name 'Aethelredus' in this shelf must be kept apart from Aelred (Ælred, also Latinized Æthelred) of Rievaulx, the twelfth-century Cistercian abbot described in the surviving records here; that man wrote spiritual treatises and histories, not the texts held under this name, so his biography does not apply. The two works printed in PL 151 are legislative and penitential documents issued in the name of King Æthelred and his wise men: codes requiring tithing of all goods, alms assessed by plowland, national fasting and public penance to avert divine wrath, and obedience to the Christian king, arguing against pagan practice and against secular priests who withheld dues.
b.s: These are royal ecclesiastical law codes from Æthelred II's England, showing how kingship, penance, and tithe obligation were fused into national legislation.

w: Ecclesiastical Laws of the Council of Greatley

b.bio: Æthelstan, son of Edward the Elder, was accepted as king by the Mercians in 924 and crowned in September 925; after conquering York in 927 he became the first Anglo-Saxon ruler of all England, and modern historians regard him as the first King of England. He centralized government, increased control over charter production, and summoned leading figures to councils that issued law. The works held under his name in PL 138 are not his own compositions but ecclesiastical laws issued in his reign: the laws of the Council of Greatley (Grately) and related provisions on tithe, church-scot, almsgiving, ordeal procedure, sorcery, and a single royal currency. They cite Archbishop Wulfhelm and earlier codes such as the Law of the English and the Law of the Mercians.
b.s: These texts show how the first king of all England legislated for the church and Christian observance as an instrument of unified rule; readers here will find early English canon-royal law on tithes, ordeals, and worship.

w: Charter for the foundation of a church

b.bio: Agano, bishop of Autun (Augustodunum), appears in the Gallia Christiana material printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina vol. 150 under the dates 1055–1098. The sources give no further biographical detail beyond his see and these dates. He is not to be confused with Stephen of Autun (bishop from 1112, died at Cluny 1139/40) or with Honorius Augustodunensis (c. 1080 – c. 1140), both later figures attached to the same city; the works held here belong to the eleventh-century bishop.
b.s: The three pieces preserved under his name — a letter on behalf of Archbishop Ralph of Tours, a church-foundation charter, and a judgment against Raginard — show an eleventh-century bishop acting in support of his metropolitan: excommunication for contumacy before ecclesiastical judgment, suspension for disobedience to church authority, and solidarity owed to the metropolitan against bishops like Gaufridus of Anjou and Count Fulco.

b.bio: Agapetus II was a Roman, elected pope on 10 May 946 after the death of Marinus II. His pontificate fell within the Saeculum obscurum: Alberic II of Spoleto ruled Rome as princeps, and Agapetus exercised little temporal power, confining himself largely to church affairs. He intervened in the disputed see of Reims, ordering a synod at Ingelheim in June 948 to resolve the claims of Hugh of Vermandois and Artald of Reims, supported Otto I's evangelization plans in the North, and joined other Italian nobles in persuading Otto to enter Italy in 951 (at Alberic's instigation). He died in Rome on 8 November 955; Alberic forced the Romans to elect his son Octavian, who became John XII.
b.s: The letters and privileges held here are instruments of papal jurisdiction: privileges protecting monasteries from episcopal and secular interference, affirming monks' right to elect their abbot under Benedict's rule, and attaching anathema to violators — addressed against figures such as Atenulf of Benevento and the archbishop of Cologne.

w: History of the Abbey of Vabres

b.bio: Agio was Archbishop of Narbonne in the early tenth century; Catholic-Hierarchy records his death as 924 and notes he consecrated Bishop Jorge in 914. Documenta Catholica Omnia dates his writings to 915–927. The library holds his History of the Abbey of Vabres (PL 132), a short text defending monastic immunity from secular jurisdiction, free election of abbots by the monks, and the claim that property-owning monks violate Benedict's rule. It also asserts royal benefaction strengthens the kingdom and names Christ king of kings.
b.s: His surviving work is a brief Carolingian charter-history of Vabres Abbey that documents monastic claims to immunity, self-governance, and exemption from the rule's property prohibition.

w: Dialogue on the Death of Saint Hathumoda

b.bio: Agius was a priest and monk of the Monastery of Corby, living in the 9th century. He was a friend of Hathumoda, first abbess of Gandersheim, and on her death in 874 wrote two works about her: a prose Life and a Dialogue on her death in elegiac verse. Other authors named Agius appear in the sources — a twentieth-century Maltese monsignor, an early twentieth-century Maltese archbishop, a Maltese parish priest — but none of them wrote these works, and they are not this man.
b.s: The works held here are the earliest accounts of Hathumoda's life and death, pairing hagiographical narrative with a verse dialogue that defends her renunciation and consolatory teaching against objecting mourners.

b.bio: the surviving records describe Andreas Agnellus of Ravenna (born c. 794/799 or 805), a ninth-century priest and titular abbot who wrote the Liber Pontificalis Ecclesiae Ravennatis, a history of Ravenna's bishops printed in PL 106. That historian left no known dogmatic treatise. The work this library holds under the name Agnellus of Ravenna is a two-page anti-Arian letter to Armenius in PL 68, arguing for the Son's eternal generation, the Father's immutability, and the Spirit's procession from Father and Son. No source here attributes that letter to the historian, so the two must be kept apart.
b.s: The single work held here is a brief polemical-exegetical letter against Arian denials of the Son's eternal generation and coequality, ending with an assertion of the Spirit's procession from both Father and Son.

w: Letters of Aimery, Patriarch of Antioch

b.bio:
Aimery of Antioch (c. 1110–1196) — Aimery of Limoges, Latin patriarch of Antioch from about 1140 until his death around 1196, was born in France around 1110, studied at Toledo, and served as archdeacon of Antioch after 1136 before his election on the deposition of Ralph of Domfront. He was the dominant churchman of the principality for half a century: after Raymond of Poitiers died in battle in June 1149 he played a leading role in the regency government; in 1153 he was imprisoned by Reynald of Châtillon over church property, released through Baldwin III's intervention, exiled to Palestine, and later restored by Reynald; and after Bohemund III's capture in 1164 Manuel Komnenos secured the prince's release on condition that a Greek be appointed to the patriarchate, displacing Aimery for a time. A scholar with sound knowledge of Greek and Latin, he corresponded with Hugh Etherian and fulfilled Pope Eugenius III's request by sending an original Greek manuscript of Chrysostom's commentary on Matthew to Rome.

Terric of the Templars (unknown) — The library prints this name over a single four-page item in PL 201, a letter circulated under Templar auspices. The manuscript tradition is difficult: the text survives on the verso of folio 15 of BnF lat. 6238, introduced as words written by 'the Templars to all the faithful of Christ,' and the identity of Terric himself remains an open question in the scholarship on that letter ('l'énigme Terric') (source:1). He should not be confused with the anonymous 'Templar of Tyre,' the 14th-century compiler of the Gestes des Chiprois, whose name rests on a designation long recognised as ungrounded (source:2). What can be said here rests on the letter itself.
b.s: The letters held here are crusading-era correspondence arguing that the eastern church needs Frankish military deliverance against Saladin and the Turks, that calamities are God's scourge for Christian sins, and that human effort avails nothing unless God looks upon us — polemic aimed also at the Greek church.

b.bio: Aimoinus, abbot of the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Pierre-sur-Dives in Normandy, wrote in Latin in the twelfth century and died in 1148. He is known chiefly for an account of miracles worked through the Virgin Mary at the first restoration of his abbey's church, a work transmitted under variant name forms (Aimon, Haymon, Haimon). The epistle held here belongs to that Marian miracle literature: it records popular devotional practices of the period, including the cart-pulling rite associated with Chartres, and asserts that invocation of Mary effects miracles and conversion.
b.s: His letter is a contemporary witness to twelfth-century Marian piety and pilgrimage rites such as the Chartres cart-pulling, and to how refusal of forgiveness was understood to exclude a person from holy fellowship.

w: On the Kings of the Franks
On the Miracles of St. Benedict
Sermon on the feasts of St. Benedict

b.bio: Aimoin was a Benedictine monk of Fleury-sur-Loire, born around 965 (Wikipedia gives c. 960); he arrived at Fleury between about 980 and 985 and died after 1008, at Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire by Arlima's account. At Abbo's suggestion he wrote the Historia Francorum, covering the Franks from earliest times to 653 and continued by later writers into the twelfth century. He completed books two and three of the Miracula Sancti Benedicti in 1005, the first book being an earlier writer's work, and in 1004 wrote the Vita Abbonis, the last of a series of lives of Fleury's abbots, all the others of which have been lost.
b.s: His history of the Franks was highly esteemed through the Middle Ages and early modern period, though its historical value is now judged slight; the works here are chiefly hagiography and national history rather than doctrinal theology.

w: Acts of the Translation of St. Savinus the Martyr
On the Miracles of St. Germanus
On the Translation of St. Vincent the Martyr
On the Translation of the Holy Martyrs
On the Translation of the Holy Martyrs George and Others

b.bio: Aimoin was a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés from before 845, later its chancellor (archivist) and chief copyist, overseeing the scriptorium from about 872, and teacher of Abbo Cernuus. His chief interests were relics and miracles, and his writings were almost entirely hagiographical. Sources disagree on his death: one gives 9 June 889, Molinier records 'after 896', and Schaff places it at the end of the ninth or beginning of the tenth century. He is not to be confused with Aimoin of Fleury, the early eleventh-century historian of the Franks.
b.s: The works held here are translationes and miracle collections — accounts of relics moved to safety from Valencia to Zaragoza, and of St. Germanus — which assert that translated relics deserve fuller veneration, that divine revelation guided the removal of Vincent's relics, that any saint's relics may substitute for the sought one, that episcopal consent is required for such translations, and that God grants better things than are asked.

b.bio: Alan of Tewkesbury was an Englishman by descent ('natione Anglus', per Gervase of Canterbury), who had earlier served as a canon at Benevento in Italy. He entered the monastery of Christ Church, Canterbury around 1174 and was elected prior in August 1179. A strong supporter of Thomas Becket against Henry II, he was removed to the abbacy of Tewkesbury, where he could less effectively resist royal encroachment; he later also served as a diplomat and judge in royal government. He died in 1202.
b.s: The works held here are letters defending Canterbury's prerogatives — against Rochester's claims to its own elections and pastoral staff, and against Robert of Hardres — together with a Life of Saint Thomas arguing for a fixed date for Becket's translation.

b.bio: None of the sourced men named Alberic matches this author. The library holds under this name a five-page sermon on St. Scholastica printed in PL 66, which places it among early Latin patristic texts; the sermon expounds the parable of the ten virgins and treats watchfulness for an hour unknown, prudence as what distinguishes wise from foolish virgins, exclusion from the wedding feast, the unity of the three persons against tritheism, and the kenosis and exaltation of the Word. Alberic of Ostia (d. 1148), Alberic of Trois-Fontaines (fl. 1230–1251), Alberic of Monte Cassino (d. 1088), and Alberic of Paris (twelfth century) are different figures and are not identified here.
b.s: The single work held here is a short patristic sermon on St. Scholastica built on the parable of the ten virgins, useful chiefly for its exegesis of watchfulness and its anti-tritheist statement on the Trinity.

b.bio: The library prints the name as Alberic of Aachen; the sources give it as Albert of Aix, Albert of Aachen, or Albericus Aquensis. He was a canon of the church of Aachen, born in the later eleventh century. He never went to the Holy Land; he compiled his history from oral and written reports of returned crusaders. Britannica dates his activity to about 1120; Wikipedia dates him fl. c. 1100 and the twelve-book Historia to between 1125 and 1150, ending its narrative in 1121. Nothing else of his life is recorded.
b.s: His Historia expeditionis Hierosolymitanae is the sole source for the People's Crusade of 1096 under Peter the Hermit and a major, if partly legendary, record of the First Crusade and the Latin Kingdom to c. 1120/1121, later used by William of Tyre.

w: Letter to the monks of Saint-Orientius of Auch

b.bio: Born at Beauvais in 1080, Alberic entered Cluny, served as prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, and was recalled by Peter the Venerable in 1126 to help restore discipline there. He was Abbot of Vézelay by 1131 before Innocent II created him Cardinal Bishop of Ostia in 1138 (consecrated 3 April 1138). As papal legate he presided over the Council of London (December 1138), mediated between Stephen and David I, acted for Eugene III against the heretic Henry of Lausanne in France, and took part in the papal elections of 1143, 1144, and 1145. Sources disagree on his death year: the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 1147 at Verdun, while Wikipedia and the Cardinals dictionary give 1148.
b.s: The library holds one letter of his, to the monks of Saint-Orientius of Auch, arguing that settlement saves reserved rights pending the abbot's consent — a document on ecclesiastical jurisdiction that the biographical sources above do not discuss.

b.bio: No surviving record identifies an author named Albert of Micy. The library holds two items under this name from PL 139: a charter and a letter addressed to Pope John XVII, which together suggest an early eleventh-century context (John XVII's pontificate is conventionally dated 1003–1004), but neither the sources nor the record give dates, offices, or biographical facts for this person. the surviving records instead describe other figures: Alpert of Metz (died 1024), Bertholdus of Micy (a ninth-century monk), Albert of Aix (fl. c. 1100), and St. Avitus, abbot of Micy (d. c. 530). None can be confidently equated with this name, so nothing further is asserted.
b.s: The works held here are a charter and a letter to John XVII whose recorded thesis is that gifts to saints procure their intercession for the donor's soul — evidence of early eleventh-century donation piety rather than of a known author's career.

b.bio: Albuinus Eremita is a Latin writer placed by the Patrologia Latina among authors of the tenth century (PL 138). The only work printed under his name there is a short letter to Heribert, archbishop of Cologne, presenting itself as a compilation drawn from the holy fathers rather than private invention. A fifteenth-century Munich manuscript (Clm 7702) transmits a 'De virtutibus religiosorum' attributed to an Albuinus heremita, though its cataloguer lists Alcuin as author.
b.s: The letter held here argues, on patristic authority, that perseverance in good works merits eternal life and that charity is the chief of all virtues.

b.bio: Alcherus de Roya is a name variant of Alcher of Clairvaux, a twelfth-century Cistercian monk of Clairvaux Abbey. Two devotional and psychological treatises were traditionally attributed to him: De diligendo Deo (On loving God) and De spiritu et anima (On Spirit and Soul). Modern scholarship doubts his authorship of both: De spiritu et anima is now dated to about 1162–1170 and read as a compilation drawing on Augustine, Alcuin, Anselm, Bernard of Clairvaux, Hugh of St Victor, Isaac of Stella, Cassiodorus, Isidore, and Boethius. Thomas Aquinas first cited it as Augustine's, then rejected the attribution, remarking that the book 'is not of great authority.'
b.s: The works held here circulated for centuries under Augustine's name and shaped scholastic teaching on the soul's rule over the body and on self-control, even after Aquinas dismissed their authority.

b.bio: Aldric (Aldericus, Audri) was born in 775 in the Gâtinais, educated at Saint-Martin of Tours, and became a monk at Ferrières. Ordained deacon in 818 and priest in 820 by Archbishop Jeremiah of Sens, he was called to the court of Louis the Pious as director of the Palace School, succeeded Adalbert as abbot of Ferrières in 821, and became archbishop of Sens in 828, being consecrated at the Council of Paris in 829. He reformed Saint-Amand and, with Ebbo, Saint-Denis, sent Servatus Lupus to study under Rabanus Maurus at Fulda, and took part in the Council of Thionville rehabilitating Louis the Pious. Sources give his death date variously as 836 (Duchesne, Levillain), 840, or 841 (Stein); he died October 10 and was buried at Ferrières.
b.s: The library holds his letters (PL 105), which defend the pastoral office — bishops dependent on others' prayers, church goods as patrimonies of the poor held in stewardship, monastic endowments immune from episcopal alienation, and abbatial election by the congregation.

w: Letter on the Son of Man

b.bio: Alexander Gemetencis (Alexandre de Jumièges) was probably a Norman, a (possibly) master at Paris and friend of Peter of Blois, who names him as his companion of studies under Peter Comestor. He was abbot of Jumièges from 1171 to 1213; the abbey chronicle calls him 'doctor divinarum et saecularium litterarum'. He may have died on 24 September and was buried in the abbey chapter. The sources here do not connect him to the eleventh-century chronicler William of Jumièges, whose biographies appear alongside his.
b.s: The library holds one short letter on the Son of Man, an exegetical quaestio arguing that Christ's self-titles are literal rather than figurative like sacraments, that 'son of man' means son of the virgin and the new Adam from the old, and that Christ alone, untithed in Abraham as sinless, recovers the heavenly inheritance Adam forfeited for all his seed.

b.bio: Alfred the Great was king of Wessex and a studious lawgiver who promulgated an important code of laws after studying the principles of lawgiving from previous codes (source:3). He spent much of his reign defending Wessex from Danish invaders, winning a great victory at the Battle of Edington in 878 and continuing to struggle with Danish advances until around 896, when the invasions ceased (source:3). The works held under this name are legal texts: ecclesiastical laws and a preface to his laws, printed in PL 138. They treat oaths and their breach, sanctuary in consecrated churches, confession, sureties, and penalties of imprisonment, exile, excommunication, and penance.
b.s: The library holds his laws rather than theological treatises: texts showing how a Christian king ordered oaths, church asylum, confession, and penance within civil legislation.

b.bio:
Alfred the Great (c. 878–c. 896) — Alfred the Great was king of Wessex and a studious lawgiver who promulgated an important code of laws after studying the principles of lawgiving from previous codes (source:3). He spent much of his reign defending Wessex from Danish invaders, winning a great victory at the Battle of Edington in 878 and continuing to struggle with Danish advances until around 896, when the invasions ceased (source:3). The works held under this name are legal texts: ecclesiastical laws and a preface to his laws, printed in PL 138. They treat oaths and their breach, sanctuary in consecrated churches, confession, sureties, and penalties of imprisonment, exile, excommunication, and penance.

Guthrum of the Anglo-Danes (d. 890) — Guthrum was a Danish leader of the Great Heathen Army who campaigned against Wessex from 871 and was defeated by Alfred the Great at Edington in 878. He submitted to baptism under the name Æthelstan, with Alfred as godfather, and ruled East Anglia as a Christian king until his death around 890. The Treaty of Alfred and Guthrum fixed the boundaries that became the foundation of the Danelaw.
b.s: The library holds his laws rather than theological treatises: texts showing how a Christian king ordered oaths, church asylum, confession, and penance within civil legislation.

b.bio: Almannus of Hautvillers was a Frankish monk, priest, and hagiographer; Wikisource gives 830–889, while Mainoldi dates him ca. 844–904. He wrote the Vita of Memmius, bishop of Châlons (BHL 5909), answering a request from Theudoinus, provost of Châlons, and addressed a letter to Archbishop Sigebod of Narbonne (873–885), possibly a dedication of a treatise De sex luminaribus.
b.s: The Rescript held here is his reply to Theudoinus prefacing the Vita Memmii, arguing that charity commands writing the saint's life, that truth outweighs elegance in sacred writing, and that saints intercede for the faithful.

b.bio: An eighth-century Alfanus, (arch)bishop of Benevento and monk of the monastery of S. Sofia there, is documented in a single dated transaction: in 781 he granted rights at Venticano. He is distinct from the better-known Alfanus I (or Alphanus), archbishop of Salerno from 1058 until his death in 1085, a translator, physician, theologian and hymnist of the eleventh century, whose career belongs to Salerno, not Benevento; a further Alphanus was abbot of St. Benedict at Salerno and attended a council of Nicholas II. The library's two-page charter under this name concerns who appoints a church's priest and the reservation of church consecrations to the bishop.
b.s: The work held here is a short charter asserting that a founder's heirs control appointment of the church's priest and that consecration of churches is reserved to the bishop — evidence of proprietary-church practice in Langobard Benevento.

w: Institution of the Cistercian Order of Saint Michael in Portugal

b.bio: Afonso Henriques, first king of Portugal (1139–1185), son of Henry of Burgundy and Teresa of León; he defeated his mother at São Mamede in 1128, won at Ourique in 1139, took Santarém and Lisbon from the Muslims in 1147 with crusader help, and secured independence from León at Valdevez, confirmed by the papal bull Manifestis Probatum. He died at Coimbra on 6 December 1185. Two other men named Alphonsus must not be confused with him here: a Hospitaller 'Frater Alphonsus de Portugalia' who appears as a master in the Order's statutes, and Alphonsus Mendez, the seventeenth-century Jesuit patriarch of Ethiopia.
b.s: The single work held under this name is a two-page account of the institution of a Cistercian order of Saint Michael in Portugal, arguing that the founding knightly fraternity honors God and the saints, that divine favor toward the kingdom requires thankful service, and that each faithful one has a guardian angel whose aid warrants perpetual commemorative institutions; it also gives the abbot sole authority to admit knights by oath, to excommunicate immoral knights, and requires knights with heirs to abstain from second marriage.

b.bio: Altfrid (also printed Altfried), third bishop of Münster from 839 and abbot of the Benedictine monastery at Werden an der Ruhr, died 22 April 849 and was buried at Werden. Probably of Frisian origin, he was a nephew of Liudger, the missionary who founded both the see of Münster and Werden, like his predecessor Gerfrid. At the request of the Werdener monks he wrote the Vita Liudgeri, though he had never known Liudger personally; he drew on good testimony and modeled the work on Alcuin's Vita Willibrordi. The work is a valuable source for the mission history of Westphalia.
b.s: The Acts of Saint Ludger held here is his Vita Liudgeri, the earliest biography of the apostle of Westphalia, arguing through narrative that the saints' examples edify more than precepts and that baptism incorporates converts into the catholic faith against pagan Saxon and Frisian practice.

b.bio: Migne's Patrologia Latina places this author in the eleventh century and prints a single letter under his name. A ninth-century archbishop of Lyon named Alwalo or Alwalonis appears in charters from Burgundy, but that man belongs to a different period and cannot be identified with the author of the epistle printed in PL 151; no source here gives biographical details for the letter-writer himself.
b.s: The letter held here is a short piece of canonistic practice on penance and excommunication: it argues that absolution may be conditional on promised satisfaction, that absolution requires a sworn surety rather than a bare promise, and that refusal of burial follows the state of excommunication.

b.bio: Amandus was a missionary bishop in the Merovingian kingdom, born near Nantes around the end of the sixth century, who evangelized Ghent and Flanders and founded monasteries at Ghent and Mount Blandin before becoming bishop of Traiecta (Maastricht). In 649 he wrote to Pope Martin I offering to resign because of heretical leanings among his clergy; Martin urged him to remain and defend orthodoxy. He died between 674 and 680. The name also belongs to an earlier presbyter who corresponded with Jerome (Letter 55, c. 393-394); that is a different man and not this author.
b.s: The work held here consists of charters recording donations to his monastery, asserting perpetual monastic ownership, burial rights, and almsgiving as treasure in heaven—primary evidence for seventh-century Frankish monastic endowment.

b.bio: Amatus (Amat d'Oloron) was bishop of Oloron from 1073 and archbishop of Bordeaux from 1089 until his death in 1101. As papal legate for Gregory VII he carried the pope's reform program into Aquitaine (1074) and Spain (1077), working with Hugh of Die against simony and clerical marriage, and supporting church independence from civil authority during the Investiture Controversy. At the Roman council of Lent 1076 he excommunicated bishops accused of simony, and he presided over the Council of Bordeaux in 1080. The works held here under his name are diplomas, conciliar acts from Bordeaux and Girona, and letters — legal documents on church property and discipline rather than theological treatises.
b.s: His texts here are instruments of the Gregorian reform in southern France: rulings securing monastic possession of churches, confirming donations, and enforcing clerical celibacy, issued against named opponents such as Duke William of Aquitaine and a simoniac abbot of Saint-Savin.

b.bio: The library prints this author as 'Amblard of Solignac'; he was a Cluniac monk who served as prior of Solignac Abbey before his election in 1115 as abbot of Saint-Martial at Limoges, an election arbitrated by Pons de Melgueil of Cluny after the deposition of Abbot Bernard. As abbot he rebuilt after the fire of 1123, received the papal legates in 1124, helped impose peace on warring Limousin lords in 1128, and attended the Council of Pisa in 1135. He died on 21 August 1143. Note: the Documenta Catholica Omnia index files him under 'Amblalardus Sollemniacensis Abbas' with a 900–1000 dating, which conflicts with the French sources' dates; the later dates are used here.
b.s: His single surviving letter here, addressed to Hervey, urges a saintly abbot to persevere in virtue and prayer amid worldly turmoil and argues that hagiography can move kings to patron monasteries.

b.bio:
Amphilochius of Iconium (c. 339/340–after 394) — Amphilochius was born around 339/340, probably at Caesarea in Cappadocia, to a distinguished family; he was likely a first cousin of Gregory of Nazianzus. Trained as a lawyer under Libanius at Antioch and practicing at Constantinople, he withdrew to the ascetic life near Gregory before Basil of Caesarea placed him as bishop of Iconium early in 374. He aided Basil in Cappadocian church affairs until Basil's death in 379, attended the Council of Constantinople in 381, summoned a council at Iconium in 376 against the Macedonians, and presided at the anti-Messalian Council of Sidon in 394. He died sometime between 394 and 403.

Ursus (unknown) — Ursus is known to this library only as the name attached to an 8-page Latin Life of Saint Basil printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 73. The work presents itself as a retranslation: it asserts that earlier Latin lives of Basil were corrupted and needed to be redone from Greek, and it explains differing saintly accounts as products of evangelistic-style omissions. None of the four saints named Ursus documented in the sources consulted — Ursus of Aosta (6th-c. evangelist), Ursus of Auxerre (bishop d. 508), Ursus of Solothurn (legendary Theban martyr), or Ursus of Ravenna (4th-c. bishop) — is credited with such a work, so no dates, office, or biography can be asserted for this author.
b.s: A close ally of Basil and Gregory against Arianism and Macedonianism, Amphilochius is chiefly remembered for his synodal letter defending the divinity of the Holy Spirit; most of his literary output is lost, so the homilies, orations, and fragments held here are among the surviving witnesses to his preaching on Christ's two natures, the resurrection, and polemic against Jews, Arians, and Eunomius.

b.bio: The work filed here under 'Anacletus (antipope)' cannot be by Pietro Pierleoni, the Roman cardinal who took the name Anacletus II at the contested papal election of 1130 and died 25 January 1138. The Letter and Privileges in PL 179 argue against Anacletus II's supporters, against Norbert of Magdeburg, and against 'the rival obedience' — that is, they come from the opposite side of the schism, the obedience of Innocent II, elected by a minority body of cardinals in the same contested election. The library's attribution is therefore to be read as naming the opponent, not the author.
b.s: This text is schism literature from the Innocentian side: it asserts that lawful election confers legitimate papal authority, that the pope rules the whole church by divine disposition, and that kings owe honor and obedience to the Roman church, while defending papal grants of episcopal liturgical insignia to abbots and the relaxation of interdicts at royal intercession.

b.bio: Anamodus was a subdeacon at Regensburg who wrote the two books of the Traditions of Saint Emmeram (Traditionum Sancti Emmerammensium Libri Duo), printed in PL 129 and dated by Documenta Catholica Omnia to 899; a Basel catalogue entry places him 'around 890'. The work is a record of gifts and exchanges of property made to the monastery of St. Emmeram, together with the disputes those transactions provoked. It names local parties on both sides — donors such as Ambricho, and opponents including Ratpreht, Scurz, Engilmunt, Tago, Rihhart, Liupger, Meio, Bernhard, and unlawful occupiers of the monastery's border — and appeals to ducal tradition and Bavarian law for the restoration of church boundaries.
b.s: The work held here is a primary source for how land was given to, contested, and recovered by a Bavarian monastery around 900, framing almsgiving and exchange as transactions that profit both parties and secure heavenly reward.

b.bio: Anastasius I was bishop of Rome from 27 November 399 until his death on 19 December 401, succeeding Siricius and preceding Innocent I. Sources disagree on some details: the Dictionary of Christian Biography gives his consecration as 398 and death as April 402, while Wikipedia, GCatholic, and Britannica give 399 and December 401. He condemned the writings of Origen shortly after their translation into Latin, called a council in 400 that judged Origen unfaithful to the Church, encouraged North African Christians against Donatism, and instructed priests to stand bowed at the reading of the Gospels. Jerome praised him as a man of great holiness. The works held here are letters connected to the Origenist controversy, including correspondence with John of Jerusalem and material on Rufinus.
b.s: His letters here document the papal condemnation of Origen and the contested case of Rufinus of Aquileia, whom Anastasius argued against but, by the record's account, passed no sentence against.

b.bio: Anastasius III was a Roman, son of a certain Lucian (some sources make him the illegitimate son of Pope Sergius III), who became bishop of Rome in 911 and died in 913. His pontificate fell under the dominance of Theophylact I of Tusculum and Theodora, leaving him little independent authority. Sources record that he evangelized the Normans of Rollo, faced Saracen threats on the Garigliano, was credited with granting privileges to ecclesiastical dioceses in Italy, and was active in settling ecclesiastical divisions in Germany — the context of the privilege printed here.
b.s: The two-page privilege held here concerns Hamburg's metropolitan jurisdiction over the northern mission churches: it grants pallium rights for specified feasts, binds papal confirmation of metropolitan sees to successors, exempts Hamburg from other metropolitans' power, and argues against the archbishop of Cologne's challenge.

b.bio: The library prints this author as 'Anastasius the Monk', and its single holding is a one-page Latin letter to Gerald on the Eucharist, printed in Migne's PL 149. This work does not match the two best-attested men named Anastasius: Anastasius Sinaita (died after 700), Greek abbot of St Catherine's Monastery on Sinai and author of the Hodegos, or Anastasius Bibliothecarius (c. 810–c. 878), papal librarian of Rome. No surviving record identifies who wrote this letter, so nothing can be asserted about his dates, office, or life.
b.s: The letter matters as a compact medieval survey of patristic eucharistic doctrine: it asserts that the consecrated elements are truly Christ's flesh and blood born of the virgin, that calling them bread remains orthodox speech, and that Augustine, Cyprian, Ambrose, Hilary, Gregory, Cyril, Leo, and Jerome agree on this.

b.bio: Andreas Bergomas was a priest of the diocese of Bergamo in the late ninth century. The sources record only two facts about him: he composed a continuation of Paul the Deacon's Historia Langobardorum down to about 877, and in 875 he helped carry the coffin of Emperor Louis II from the Oglio river as far as the Adda. He never states that he came from Bergamo, nor does he identify himself as Lombard or Frank. His chronicle summarizes Paul the Deacon from the Lombard arrival under Alboin to Liutprand, then becomes an original account of high politics: the Carolingian rulers of northern Italy and Louis II's campaigns in southern Italy.
b.s: His Chronicle is the best source for the succession dispute after Louis II's death and an important primary source for ninth-century Italy, especially the Po Valley; the library holds it as a short text treating providence, sin, baptism, the church, and last things through Lombard history.

b.bio: The library prints this name for the author of the Chronicon of the church of Cambrai (PL 149), a Latin chronicle transmitted under the title S. Andreae Castri Cameracensi Chronicon. The author's identity is not established by the sources at hand; the Documenta Catholica Omnia edition lists the work as anonymous. What can be said comes from the text itself: it narrates the affairs of the diocese of Cambrai in the age of the Investiture Contest, naming Countess Richildis, Pope Calixtus, and Emperor Henry IV among its subjects.
b.s: The Chronicle held here is a contemporary account of the church of Cambrai during the imperial-papal conflict, treating episcopal office, persecution, monastic reform, and providential rule through history and polemic against partisans of Henry IV.

w: Miracles of Benedict from the History by Andrew the Monk

b.bio: The library prints this name as Andreas Fontis Ebraldi: Andrew, a monk of Fontevraud, the abbey in Anjou founded by Robert of Arbrissel in 1101 as a double house — a community of monks (Saint-Jean-l'Habit) beside the nuns' monastery (the Grand Moutier), all under an abbess's authority. The Légendiers latins database records him, with a question mark on his identity, as the author of a De ultimis diebus et obitu of Robert of Arbrissel (BHL 7260). Nothing in the sources gives his dates or offices beyond his monastic status at Fontevraud.
b.s: His works here are the Second Life of Robert of Arbrissel and Miracles of Benedict drawn from Andrew's history — primary evidence for how Fontevraud understood its founder, its subjection of the monks to the nuns, and the securing of its constitution during Robert's lifetime.

b.bio: The library prints this name over a single page of ecclesiastical constitutions in PL 151, directed against pagan practice among the Scythians and prescribing restoration of Christian worship, obedience to bishops, expiation for homicide, and penalties including death for despising the constitution. The sources consulted describe several distinct men who bore the name Andreas Ungarus or Hungarus: a thirteenth-century Hungarian priest and diplomat at the courts of Béla IV and Charles of Anjou, author of the Descriptio victoriae a Karolo Provinciae comite reportate; the fifteenth-century Carthusian Andreas Pannonius, commentator on the Song of Songs; and a hypothetical Andreas Hungarus, archbishop of Bar from 1307, proposed as author of the Descriptio Europae Orientalis. None of these is linked to the constitutions printed here, so no identification can be made.
b.s: The single page held here is a brief legislative-polemical text on converting a pagan people, valuable chiefly as evidence of how church discipline and civil penalty were joined in mission territory.

b.bio: Andrew of Strumi, born at Parma in the first half of the eleventh century, was a disciple of the deacon Arialdo in the Milanese campaign against simoniacal clergy under Archbishop Guido of Velate, and recovered Arialdo's body after his murder. He joined the Vallombrosans around 1069, knew their founder John Gualbert, and became abbot of Strumi about 1085. He mediated between Florence and Arezzo during the papal-imperial schism. A reference in his Life of John Gualbert to a miracle datable only after 1106 casts doubt on the traditional death date of March 10, 1097.
b.s: The work held here is his Vita of John Gualbert, an eyewitness-adjacent account of the Vallombrosan founder that frames the order's fight against simoniac bishops as a matter of publicly confessed truth and grace-given vocation.

b.bio: Angilram (as printed here, Angelram) was a Frankish prelate of noble Austrasian stock who succeeded Chrodegang as bishop of Metz, consecrated 25 September 768, and served until his death in October 791. From 784 he was archchaplain at Charlemagne's court, with a papal dispensation to remain there permanently; by 788 he held the honorary title of archbishop and served concurrently as abbot of Chiemsee, Senones and Sint-Truiden. He commissioned Paul the Deacon's history of the bishops of Metz and an early single-volume Bible of the Carolingian Renaissance (lost in 1944). His historical importance rests largely on the canon-law collection bearing his name, the Capitula Angilramni, a component of the pseudo-Isidorian corpus defending bishops against civil tribunals.
b.s: The works under his name here — charters of donation securing monasteries against advocates, and a collection of canons on episcopal rights — belong to the Carolingian defense of episcopal authority that later fed the pseudo-Isidorian decretals.

b.bio: Enguerran (Angelran or Angelrannus), called the Wise, was born at Saint-Riquier around 975 and trained under Fulbert of Chartres in music and dialectic. He became abbot of Centula (Saint-Riquier), where Duke Richard II of Normandy addressed a charter to him between 1010 and 1017 granting the church of Equemauville at his request; Archbishop Robert of Rouen also gave him a pallium. Late in life he was paralyzed but defended the abbey's rights against usurpers and King Henry I. He died on 9 December 1045.
b.s: The library holds his versified Life of Saint Richarius, a hagiographic poem defending verse as dutiful recitation of scripture and arguing that reading saints' lives inflames love of God.

w: On the Restoration of the Monastery of Saint-Riquier

b.bio: A Frankish noble educated at Charlemagne's palace school at Aachen under Alcuin, Angilbert served the court as secretary, diplomat, and poet — his academy nickname was Homer — and accompanied Pepin to Italy as primicerius palatii. He carried the Frankish Synod of Frankfurt's document on images to Pope Adrian I and was sent on several embassies to Rome (Wikipedia gives 792, 794, and 796). Sources differ on his birth year: Britannica gives c. 740 at Aachen, Wikipedia c. 760; and on when he was named abbot of Centula: New Advent gives 790, Britannica 794. He rebuilt the monastery sumptuously, endowed it with a library of some 200 volumes, and hosted Charlemagne there in 800. He died 18 February 814 and is venerated as a saint.
b.s: The works held here center on his account of rebuilding Saint-Riquier — its three churches dedicated by twelve bishops, its authenticated relics recorded by name, and its endowed community maintained in perpetuity — alongside letters, poems, and statutes.

w: Verses on the Book of St. Augustine to Louis

b.bio: A Frankish noble educated at Charlemagne's palace school under Alcuin, who nicknamed him 'Homer' for his verse. He served as primicerius palatii to King Pepin in Italy, carried the Frankish position on images to Pope Adrian I, and made several embassies to Rome. Sources differ on his birth year (Wikipedia c. 760, Britannica c. 740); he died 18 February 814. Named abbot of Centula around 790/794, he rebuilt the monastery and endowed it with a library of some 200 volumes.
b.s: The work held here is a short metrical exegesis asserting that God created all things in measure, number, and weight and sustains them by his power — a Carolingian court poet's Latin verses on creation and providence addressed to Louis.

b.bio: Angilbertus Pusterla is Angilbert II, Archbishop of Milan from 27 or 28 June 824 until his death on 13 December 859, successor to Angilbert I and called Angilberto da Pusterla. He counselled King Lothair I against Emperor Louis the Pious in 833, then served as intermediary between Lothair and Louis in 837, acted as missus dominicus in 844 and May 859, attended the Synod of Pavia in 850, and championed the deacon Anspert's cause on 20 June 857. He donated the golden altar of Sant'Ambrogio and funded the basilica's renovation. The Frankish courtier-poet Angilbert, abbot of Saint-Riquier (d. 814), is a different man.
b.s: The two texts held here — a rescript to Emperor Louis and a privilege for the Ambrosian Basilica — show him defending episcopal authority: lawful election by clergy and people with episcopal fallback, accused clergy owed legitimate hearing and punishment, negligent clergy granted time for amendment, no ordination for kinship favor or money, and resistance to lay proprietors of private basilicas.

b.bio: The library prints this name as Aeneas Sylvius and shelves a single work, 'Calendar of Silvius', in PL 50. This is not Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini (1405–1464), the humanist diplomat who became Pope Pius II; all available biographical sources describe that later man, whose dates and offices do not match an author in the Latin Fathers series. Nothing can be asserted here about the compiler beyond what the library record shows.
b.s: The single work held here is a 'Calendar of Silvius' preserved in PL 50; its content and usefulness cannot be further characterized on the basis of the available evidence.

b.bio: Annemund (also Ennemond or Dalfinus) succeeded Viventius as archbishop of Lyon between 652 and 654, during the reign of Clovis II, and served as a royal councillor. Bede records that he received Wilfrid of York hospitably at Lyon in 653, offered him the government of a large part of Gaul, and later gave him the tonsure. He was put to death — Bede attributes the order to Queen Balthild, though most modern scholars blame Ebroin, mayor of the palace — after being slandered as a traitor and summoned to court; his body was returned to Lyon.
b.s: The library holds only a single-page charter under his name from PL 87; his historical importance rests on his martyrdom and his role in Wilfrid's early career rather than on writings.

b.bio: Anno II was born around 1010 at Altsteußlingen in Swabia to the Steusslingen family and educated at Bamberg, where he headed the cathedral school. Chaplain to Emperor Henry III from 1046, he became provost of Goslar in 1054 and Archbishop of Cologne in 1056. He led the abduction of the young Henry IV in 1062 and acted as regent of the empire from 1063 to 1065. He founded monasteries, including Michaelsberg at Siegburg, died on 4 December 1075 at Siegburg, and was canonized on 29 April 1183 by Pope Lucius III.
b.s: The library holds his diplomas (PL 143): charters recording church endowments — including a donation of a castle to St. Peter of Cologne with a forfeiture clause protecting the queen's usufruct — asserting that God's will grants church possessions, forbidding alienation of donated property, binding serfs to altars by perpetual census, and recording the foundation of a monastery with papal and imperial permission, exempt from secular service under anathema.

b.bio: Ansgar (Anskar), born near Amiens on 8 September 801 and died at Bremen on 3 February 865, was brought up in the Benedictine monastery of Corbie, sent as a missionary to Denmark and Sweden, and made Archbishop of Hamburg, later of the united see of Hamburg-Bremen. His successor Rimbert wrote his life (Vita Ansgarii), which records his Scandinavian missions and visions. The library holds under his name the Life of Willehad, first bishop of Bremen, and an epistle; these treat the conversion of the pagan Frisians, the veneration of saints, and missionaries sent with the consent of king and bishops.
b.s: Known as the Apostle of the North, he organized the Frankish mission to Scandinavia; the works here are hagiographical and epistolary texts presenting saints' lives as models for imitation and their patronage as warranting veneration.

b.bio: Ansellus (also Ancellus), a secular cleric who studied at Paris around 1084–1088 and later served as cantor of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem. Around 1108–1120 he wrote to Bishop Gerbert and Archdeacon Stephen of Paris, thanking the cathedral chapter for his schooling and sending relics of the True Cross with an account of how the cross was divided into fragments so the Saracens could not burn it. The library holds one of these letters (PL 162).
b.s: His letters are firsthand evidence of relic circulation between crusader Jerusalem and Paris, arguing that many signs of Jesus are unwritten in scripture, that dividing relics preserves them from destruction, and that fragments of the True Cross survive in many churches.

b.bio: The sources place Ansellus Scholasticus in the eleventh century and give no birthplace, office, or dates beyond that. He is not Anselm of Canterbury, nor any other better-known Anselmus; the name here attaches to items in Migne's Patrologia Latina, volume 151. The library holds his Vision (Visio), printed from the Poesies Latines Populaires (PL 151, cols. 643-652), a short visionary text in Latin verse that cites Gregory. Documenta Catholica Omnia also lists a one-column Vita Operaque drawn from Mansi (PL 151, col. 643), which is biographical notice rather than an independent work.
b.s: His sole surviving piece is a brief eleventh-century Latin vision text, of interest chiefly as evidence for popular Latin visionary poetry of the period.

b.bio: Anselm IV (Anselmo da Bovisio) was consecrated archbishop of Milan on 3 November 1097, having been elected bishop of Brescia that year after entering the monastery of S. Lorenzo. He held a reforming synod on 5–7 April 1098 that condemned simony and affirmed the excommunication of imperially appointed bishops, accepting the acts of his predecessor Anselm III but not those of Tedald. A close friend of Urban II, he was recruited by Paschal II to lead the Crusade of 1101, preached it throughout Lombardy, led its Lombard contingent, and died on 30 September 1101 while on the expedition.
b.s: The work held here is a set of privileges confirming the rights of the monastery of St. Protasius under its abbot against its neighbors and the abbot of St. Simplicianus, an example of episcopal canonical judgment settling Milanese church disputes.

w: History of the Dedication of the Church of Saint Remigius

b.bio: A Benedictine monk of the abbey of Saint-Remi at Reims, active around 1050. Nothing else is known of his life except that he wrote in 1056, at the wish of his priest, a history of the dedication of the rebuilt church of Saint-Remigius by Pope Leo IX in October 1049, including an account of Leo's journey to Reims and the council held there on 2–3 October 1049. The work was known to Sigebert of Gembloux as the pope's itinerary for this journey. He is not Anselm of Laon or Anselm of Liège.
b.s: His history is a primary witness to Leo IX's Reims council of 1049 and the dedication of the church of Saint-Remigius, including its canons against simony, clerical marriage, and contumacious clergy.

b.bio: Anselmus de Ribodimonte is Anselm of Ribemont, a Flemish nobleman and castellain of Bouchain, Ostrevant and Valenciennes, son of a father killed at the battle of Cassel (1071). He joined the First Crusade in the army of Robert II of Flanders with Eustace III of Boulogne, mortgaging lands to finance the journey. He was a friend of Archbishop Manasses II of Reims, founder of the monastery of Ribemont, and died at Arqa on 25 February 1099. His letters to Manasses are eyewitness accounts of the crusade; the library holds one such letter.
b.s: His letter to Manasses II of Reims is a firsthand report from the crusade, attributing victory over Corbaran and the Turks to God's favor, intercessory prayer, confession, and the eucharist rather than knightly merit.

b.bio: Antoninus Honoratus was bishop of Constantina, also called Cirta, in the Roman province of Africa. Around 437 he wrote a letter to Arcadius, a Spaniard and former friend of the Vandal king Genseric, who had been banished for refusing Arianism; three other exiled bishops are addressed with him. The letter exhorts them to endure suffering for Christ, and Arcadius was afterwards martyred. It is cited as evidence for Genseric's promotion of Arianism.
b.s: The library holds his single surviving work, a letter of consolation to exiled confessors under Vandal persecution, arguing that martyrdom brings remission of all sins and that the soul sees Christ at death before the resurrection.

b.bio: The name 'Antoninus of Piacenza' as printed here conflates two figures: a martyr of Piacenza who died in AD 303 under Diocletian, and an anonymous sixth-century pilgrim from Piacenza whose itinerarium was long misattributed to that martyr. The Itinerary held in this library is the pilgrim's work: it opens by invoking blessed Antoninus the martyr as companion and patron of the journey, which fueled the confusion. The author travelled from Piacenza via Constantinople and Cyprus to Tripolis, then through Galilee, Samaria, the Jordan, Jerusalem, Gaza, and toward Sinai in the 570s.
b.s: His Itinerary is a primary witness to Byzantine-era holy places and relic cults, including early attestations of the veneration of the onyx chalice at the Holy Sepulchre and the Holy Lance on Mount Zion; the pages held here report miracles at Christ's baptism site in the Jordan and healings at the Dead Sea.

b.bio: Surviving records do not clearly identify this author: they cover Anthony of Padua (d. 1231), Anthony Sandini (1692–1751), and Anthony of the Mother of God (d. 1641), none of whom fits a Latin patristic poet printed in Migne's fifth volume; they are different people of the same name and are not used here. The library record alone identifies him: an anonymous or obscure Christian writer whose eleven-page poem attacks pagan religion, arguing that Christian doctrine surpasses pagan philosophical wisdom, cataloguing the incests and bestial transformations of Jupiter (including his rape of Proserpina as a serpent), and dismissing Cynic asceticism as ostentation rather than true wisdom. He cites Paulinus, Virgil, Tertullian, Augustine, Ovid, Macrobius, Vonckius, and Muratorius most frequently.
b.s: His poem here is a compact late-antique polemic against paganism, marshalling classical citations to expose pagan myth as immoral and philosophy as inferior to Christian teaching.

b.bio: No surviving record describes an author named Anthony of Seville whose life or dates can be stated here. The sources given instead cover St. Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636) and Anthony of the Mother of God (1583–1637), a Discalced Carmelite of Salamanca and Alcalá; neither matches the work held under this name, so neither career may be attached to it. What the library record does show is that the single work printed under this name in PL 136 is a short critical inquiry into the authenticity of early Spanish historical texts.
b.s: The work held here is a citation-survey and polemic testing the genuineness of ancient Spanish chronicles, directed chiefly against the forgeries associated with Jerónimo Román de la Higuera (Hieronymus Romanus de la Higuera) and the pseudo-Liutprand and pseudo-Dexter texts they produced.

b.bio: Anthony was born at Coma near Heracleopolis Magna in Egypt to well-to-do Christian parents. Around age eighteen or twenty he gave away his inheritance after hearing the Gospel call to perfection and withdrew into the Egyptian desert about AD 270, living as a hermit though many sought him as a teacher. Athanasius' Life of Anthony, received as substantially historical, made him known across the Christian world as a model for monks.
b.s: The work held here is a short collection of rules and precepts on prayer, fasting, humility, and avoidance of temptation, transmitted under his name in Migne's Patrologia Latina.

b.bio: Antonius was a Greek monk who knew Simeon Stylites closely and wrote a life of his master around the year 460. The work survives only in a Latin translation published by Bolland in the Acta Sanctorum (i. p. 264); Leo Allatius reports having seen a Greek manuscript. Vossius, knowing only the Latin, hesitated over whether Antonius should be counted a Latin or Greek historian.
b.s: His Life of Saint Simeon is an eyewitness account of the pillar ascetic, presenting Simeon's endurance as imitating Job's suffering, his miracles as converting the nations to faith, and his cross-signing as routing demons.

b.bio: The library holds one work under this name, a sermon addressed to the Archbishop of Rouen, printed in PL 147. No surviving record identifies which archdeacon of Rouen wrote it; the sources describe archbishops of Rouen (Hugh of Amiens, William Bona Anima) rather than any archdeacon author, so they do not settle the attribution. What can be said is what the text itself shows: a Norman ecclesiastic writing to his metropolitan on penitence.
b.s: The sermon here treats penitence as a pastoral office: bishops mediate for lapsed sinners, the keys bind and loose in baptism and penance, and humble confession cleanses sin beyond snow.

w: Address for the reconciliation of penitents

b.bio: The library holds one work under this name: an address for the reconciliation of penitents printed in PL 55 among the appendix material following Leo the Great's sermons. The author is identified only by the title 'archdeacon'; no source supplies his name, see, or dates. The three sources attached to this record describe later medieval figures who bore the same designation — Ralph de Diceto (archdeacon of Middlesex), Guido de Baysio ('the Archdeacon' of Bologna), and Ricardus Anglicus (archdeacon of Bologna) — none of whom wrote patristic sermons on penance; they are different persons and are disregarded here.
b.s: The address argues that remission of sins has become more generous through indulgence, that penitents' tears wash as baptismal waters wash, and that the bishop's intercession restores the fallen through divine reconciliation — a witness to how early Latin practice joined baptismal imagery to public penance.

w: Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane

b.bio: Ardo Smaragdus entered the monastery of Aniane as a boy, probably as an oblate, and was brought up under Abbot Benedict of Aniane. Ordained a priest, he headed the monastery school and in 794 accompanied Benedict to the Council of Frankfurt. In 814 he succeeded Benedict as abbot when the latter took up residence at the imperial court at Aix-la-Chapelle under Louis the Pious. At the request of the monks of Cornelimünster, where Benedict had died, he wrote a life of his master in 822, one of the more reliable hagiographical works of its period. He was honored as a saint at Aniane after his death there in March 843.
b.s: His life of Benedict of Aniane is the principal contemporary witness to the monk whose reform shaped Carolingian monasticism, and it is what this library holds under his name.

b.bio: Aregius of Gap (also printed Aredius, Arigius, Arey) was bishop of Gap in the late sixth century. The sources disagree on his dates: the BBKL gives birth around 540 and death 604/608 (episcopate 574/579–604/608), while Wikipedia places his birth around 575 and death around 605, and Catholic Online gives his death as 604 after twenty years as bishop. He is venerated as a saint with a feast on May 1 (Catholic Online; also other feasts per BBKL). The library holds a life and testament printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 72; Duchesne considered the earliest life contemporary.
b.s: The works here are a hagiographic life and testament of an early bishop of Gap, preserved in PL 72.

w: Two sermons to the clergy of Milan

b.bio: Arialdus (Arialdo) of Carimate was a deacon of noble birth, born c. 1010 at Cutiacum (Cucciago), near Como. After studying at Laon and Paris he was made a canon in Milan. There he led the Pataria, a movement against the simoniacal and married clergy of the city, alongside Anselm of Baggio (later Pope Alexander II). Archbishop Guido of Velate excommunicated him; Pope Stephen IX reinstated him and ordered him to continue the reform. He was later seized by Guido's partisans, confined to an island in Lake Maggiore, and assassinated by two priests. Alexander II subsequently declared him a martyr.
b.s: The library holds his two sermons to the clergy of Milan (PL 143), documents of the eleventh-century campaign for clerical reform that preceded the wider Gregorian movement.

b.bio: Aribo the Scholastic was a Benedictine monk and scholasticus at the abbey of St. James in Liège, active around the middle of the eleventh century. His origins are unrecorded; a supposed connection with Freising is unfounded. Between about 1060 and 1075 he wrote his two-part treatise De musica, dedicated to Bishop Ellenhard of Freising: the first part sets out his own theory of music and its relation to the universe; the second is a critical commentary on Guido of Arezzo's teaching. He also built instruments and devised a measuring device for organ pipes, named after him the Aribuncala.
b.s: The work held here is his De musica, notable for the caprea, a diagram superimposing modal tetrachords on the gamut that allowed swifter measurement on the monochord, and for its critical engagement with Guido of Arezzo and other moderns on mode, figure, and monochord practice.

w: On the book 'On Interpretation' by Aristotle

b.bio:
Aristotle (c. 475–7 – 526?) — The six works shelved under 'Aristotle' are not by Aristotle: they are the Latin commentaries of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius preserved in PL 64 — on the Categories, On Interpretation, Prior and Posterior Analytics, Topics, and Sophistical Refutations. Boethius was a Roman aristocrat born c. 475–7 C.E., died 526? C.E., living most of his life under Theoderic. He translated Aristotle's logical works into Latin and wrote commentaries on them as well as logical textbooks, drawing extensively on Greek Neoplatonists such as Porphyry and Iamblichus. The theses recorded here — on contradiction, negation, and enunciation — belong to his exegesis of Aristotle's logic, not to Aristotle's own text.
