Boethius (c. 475–480 – 524–526) — Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, born in Rome into the patrician Anicii family, was orphaned young and raised by Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, whose daughter Rusticiana he married. He served the Ostrogothic king Theoderic as senator, consul, and magister officiorum before his execution at Pavia around 524–526; the diocese of Pavia honors him as a martyr on 23 October (cult sanctioned 1883). Sources differ slightly on his dates: Wikipedia gives c. 480–524, the Stanford Encyclopedia c. 475–7 to 526?, Routledge c. 480–525/6. His project of translating Greek logic into Latin made him a principal conduit between ancient philosophy and the medieval Latin West.
b.s: These commentaries were a principal channel through which Aristotle's logic reached the Latin Middle Ages; a reader holding them holds Boethius's own teaching, not Aristotle's.

b.bio:
Armenius (unknown) — The library prints this author as 'Armenius' and holds under the name a Latin patristic piece in PL 74 treating the Trinity, Christology, and baptism. the surviving records describe two different men who do not match that record: an early Christian priest Armenius who wrote in Greek an account of the martyrdom of Chrysanthus and Daria (published only in Surius's Latin translation), and Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609), the Dutch Reformed theologian of Leiden. Neither is the author of the work shelved here, so no dates or biography can be asserted for the writer the library actually holds.

Honorius the Monk (c. 1106–1156) — The sources identify this author with Honorius Augustodunensis ('Honorius of Autun'), a twelfth-century theologian who called himself 'ecclesiae presbyter et scholasticus' and deliberately concealed his real name behind a pseudonym. He was certainly a monk, spent time in England as a student of Anselm, worked mainly in southern Germany, and was at the Irish monastery (Scots Monastery) at Regensburg toward the end of his life. His birthplace is disputed: candidates include Autun, Augst near Basle, Augsburg, and Canterbury.
b.s: The single work held here is a doctrinal definition-and-polemic asserting three coeternal coequal persons in one substance, the eternal generation of the Son, one person subsisting in two natures, and baptism as conferring grace and remission.

b.bio: Arnaud (Arnaldus) was abbot of the Benedictine abbey of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif at Sens from 1096 to 1124. Around 1108 he commissioned the writing of the abbey's chronicle and the copying of its documents; the anonymous work long misattributed to a monk 'Clarius' is in fact tied to his abbacy. The letter preserved in PL 163 is a petition to Daimbert, archbishop of Sens, and the lord bishop of Langres, arguing that love of neighbor is Christ's chief commandment and that lepers may lawfully be relocated away from settled lands — a position contested by Bernard, abbot of Saint-Jean-de-Réome, and his monks at Troyes.
b.s: His surviving letter is a rare early-twelfth-century record of a jurisdictional dispute over the segregation of lepers, pitting episcopal petition against monastic opposition.

b.bio: Arnobius Afer (Arnobius the Elder, of Sicca) was a Numidian rhetorician who taught at Sicca Veneria under Diocletian. A pagan convert — Jerome says conversion followed a dream — he was suspected by the local bishop and wrote the seven-book Adversus nationes (c. 303) as a pledge of his conviction. Jerome calls it Adversus gentes; the title Adversus nationes comes from the sole surviving ninth-century manuscript. He was teacher of Lactantius. Beyond Jerome's notices and the treatise itself, nothing of his life is transmitted.
b.s: His Adversus nationes is a major pre-Constantinian Latin apology answering the pagan charge that Christians caused calamities, attacking idolatry, anthropomorphism, and pagan myth while defending monotheism and the divinity of Christ.

b.bio: Arnold (Arnulf) of Halberstadt was a tenth-century German prelate, one of the principal feudal bishops of Germany and leader of the imperial forces against Boleslaw of Poland; he died on 7 September 1023. The letter held here is addressed to Henry of Würzburg and concerns an episcopal dispute: it defends an ordination confirmed by many authorities against annulment, argues that refusal of consent makes schism within the church, and presses obedience to ordained power, dividing bishoprics only by holy precedent for souls' sake.
b.s: His single surviving letter here is a concrete case of Ottonian episcopal jurisdiction and church-order polemic between bishops.

w: Treatise on the Schism Arisen after the Death of Honorius II

b.bio: Arnulf of Lisieux was born in Normandy, a second son of Hardouin de Neuville, educated by his brother Jean, bishop of Sées, probably studied theology in Paris, and by 1133 was a clerk in the household of Geoffrey of Lèves, bishop of Chartres, studying Roman law in Bologna. He made his name with a violent letter defending Pope Innocent II against Gerard of Angoulême, a partisan of the antipope Anacletus II (Petrus Leonis). Raised to the see of Lisieux in 1141, he began repairing and later rebuilding its cathedral, went on crusade with Louis VII in 1147, and remained faithful to Pope Alexander III at the Council of Tours in 1163 during that later schism.
b.s: The work held here is his polemic against Girard of Angoulême and the Pierleoni party in the schism following the death of Honorius II, arguing that lawful election and consent mark the true pope while the false shepherd persecutes the church under pretense.

b.bio: The library holds under this name a single two-page letter to Milo (PL 179), an account of a victory over the Saracens. It attributes the success of the crusade fleet to divine blessing, argues that God grants victory in holy war and works wonders through his saints, and grounds all things in God. It also treats sacraments, true worship and last things, and argues against the Saracens. No dates or biographical details are attested for this author. Other writers named Arnulf appear in the consulted sources — Arnulf of Orléans, grammarian of the late twelfth century; Arnulf of Milan, chronicler fl. 1018–1077; Arnulf of Lisieux, bishop 1104/1109–1184 — but none is identified with this letter, so they are set aside.
b.s: His one surviving piece here is a brief crusading letter that reads a military victory over the Saracens as wrought by divine rather than human agency.

w: Deeds of the Archbishops of Milan

b.bio: Arnulf of Milan was a Milanese historian, great-nephew of Archbishop Arnulf I of Milan and a member of the aristocratic Capitani class. His Liber gestorum recentium (written 1072–1077), held here as the Deeds of the Archbishops of Milan, is a contemporary account beginning with King Hugh of Arles in 925 and ending in 1077 with Rudolf of Rheinfelden's election as anti-king. He wrote as an eyewitness or from testimony he judged credible. Though of aristocratic background, he sided with papal reform and Gregory VII against simoniac clergy, while resisting the appointment of Archbishop Atto; after Canossa he joined the mission promising loyalty to Atto.
b.s: His chronicle is a primary source for the Gregorian Reform, the Patarene movement, and the Investiture Controversy as seen from Milan.

b.bio: Arnulf, illegitimate son of King Lothair of France and a Carolingian, was made archbishop of Reims by Hugh Capet in March 989, against the wishes of his predecessor Adalberon. In September 989 he backed his uncle Charles of Lower Lorraine's bid for the throne; imprisoned in 990, he was deposed for treason at the Council of Reims in June 991 in favor of Gerbert of Aurillac. Pope John XV's legate presided over synods at Mouzon on 2 June and 1 July 995 that declared the deposition invalid, and Arnulf was reinstated, holding the see until his death. Sources give the year of death as 1021 (Wikipedia/Wikidata) or about 1023 (McClintock and Strong). The works held here are not his letters on the schism but privileges, oaths, anathemas, a commonitorium, and a little book of abdication defending monastic property and donors.
b.s: The texts here show the archbishop as a defender of monasteries against plunderers at Reims and officials of Mouzon, asserting that donated property is perpetual, immune from reclamation, and remedies the donor's soul.

w: Letter on the Doctrine of Living a Life

b.bio: Arnulf de Boeriis (Arnulfus de Boeriis, Arnoul de Bohéries) was a Cistercian monk of the diocese of Laon who died in 1149, according to Biblissima citing BnF data; Documenta Catholica Omnia places him broadly in the twelfth century. The library holds five short ascetical texts printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volumes 180 and 184, headed by the Speculum monachorum (PL 184, cols. 1175-1178), whose incipit and explicit are recorded by Arlima from Paris, BnF espagnol 353; the Speculum monachorum appears twice in the library's holdings (a second copy under PL 180).
b.s: His Speculum monachorum is a compact twelfth-century manual of monastic self-examination, prescribing weekly confession and inward correction of thoughts, words, and deeds; the other works here extend the same program of prayer, meditation on Christ's passion, and discipline against temptation.

b.bio: Arsinus de Albione appears in the library's record only as the author of a single donation text in PL 151, in which he gives an estate to a monastery in perpetuity, invoking Urban II and Abbot Raymund of Albion. the surviving records here describe other men of similar name: Arsenius the Great (d. c. 450), the fourth-century Roman deacon turned Desert Father, and Arsenius Apostolius, the Cretan-born bishop of Monemvasia (c. 1468–1538). Neither matches this eleventh- or twelfth-century Latin donor, so their biographies are set aside.
b.s: His single held work is a charter-style history recording the perpetual donation of an estate to a monastery, useful as evidence of monastic endowment practice under Urban II.

b.bio: Artaldus, printed here as Arthaldus of Reims, was a Benedictine monk of Saint-Remi at Reims whom King Ralph placed in the archbishopric in 931 or 932, displacing the child Heribert son of the Count of Vermandois. He crowned Louis IV at Laon in 936 and excommunicated Count Heribert II of Vermandois; in 940 Heribert and Hugh the Great drove him from Reims by force, and Hugh son of Heribert was consecrated bishop at Soissons. Louis IV and Otto I restored him in 946, and synods at Verdun (947) and Ingelheim (948) ratified his return. He later served as royal chancellor and crowned Lothair in 954.
b.s: The epistle held here is his polemic against Count Heribert and the bishops gathered at Soissons, asserting that election of bishops belongs to clergy and people, that ordination without the rightful bishop's consent is invalid, that no consecration may occur while a legitimate bishop lives, that coerced abdication is void with appeal to Rome, and that pallium and ministry must not be surrendered even for life.

b.bio:
Ascaricus (d. 810/11) — Ascaricus was a bishop in the northwest of the Iberian Peninsula, either of Astorga or of Braga, who died in 810 or 811. Pope Hadrian I condemned him for adoptionism in a letter written between 785 and 791, probably 786. His Epistula ad Tuseredum, explaining the resurrection of the body, places him in the Kingdom of Asturias; he also wrote a poem to Tuseredo modelled on Prudentius's Hamartigenia and the verse of Sedulius. He should not be confused with Ascaric, fourth bishop of Palencia (c. 639–673), a Visigothic signatory of the Eighth Council of Toledo.

Tusaredus (fl. 8th c.) — Wikisource records Tusaredus as a cleric whose activity falls in the eighth century; it gives no dates, see, or offices beyond that. The letters preserved under his name in PL 99 are polemical pieces directed against schismatics and dissenters — including dissenters who appealed to Isidore and some who blasphemed against Mary — defending the resurrection of the saints with Christ in glorified bodies, preaching Christ crucified over cunning speculation, and attributing schism and heresy to vice and the devil. He cites Jerome, Gregory, Isidore, and Augustine heavily.
b.s: His letter on the resurrection of the body is one of the few surviving theological works from the Asturian kingdom, written amid the adoptionist controversy and local schism.

b.bio:
Athalaricus rex (c. 516 – 2 October 534) — Athalaric succeeded his grandfather Theodoric the Great as king of the Ostrogoths in Italy in 526, aged about ten. His mother Amalasuintha held real power as regent throughout his reign; Procopius describes him as living dissolutely, and he died on 2 October 534, still a teenager. The documents printed under his name in PL 72 are royal letters and edicts from the Variae of Cassiodorus, including a letter to the Roman clergy and an edict of 533 recognizing the pope as head of all bishops.

Amalasuntha Gothorum (c. 494/5–535) — Amalasuntha, daughter of Theodoric the Great, was born around 494/5–498 (sources differ) and ruled the Ostrogothic kingdom from 526 to 535, first as regent for her son Athalaric and then as queen regnant. Educated in Greek, Gothic, and Latin, she pursued a pro-Byzantine policy and patronized Roman learning, drawing opposition from Gothic nobles; she was deposed and killed in 535 after about six months of sole rule, an event Justinian used as grounds for invading Italy. The volume printed under her name in Migne is a citation-survey that cites Cassiodorus.

Theodahadus Ostrogoth (c. 480–536) — Theodahad was king of the Ostrogoths from late 534 until his death in December 536. He first ruled jointly with his cousin Amalasuintha, who elevated him after the death of her son Athalaric; seeking sole power, he had her imprisoned and murdered around April 30, 535. His deposition and death while fleeing Witiges ended a reign widely judged a failure: his murder of Amalasuintha gave Justinian I the pretext for the Gothic War, and he proved ineffective against Belisarius's invasion. The work held under his name in PL 72 is citation-survey material drawing on Cassiodorus.
b.s: The works held here are not the king's own writing but the official acts of his reign as drafted by Cassiodorus — state papers that show how an Arian Gothic monarchy addressed the Roman church.

b.bio: Atto was born around 1070, at Badajoz according to Flórez and the Catholic Encyclopedia, or Beja by a Portuguese source. A pilgrim to Italy, he stopped at Vallombrosa Abbey where he was welcomed by Abbot Bernardo degli Uberti; by 1100 he was a monk there, became abbot in 1105 and abbot-general around 1120. He was made Bishop of Pistoia — appointed 1133 according to Wikipedia, 1135 according to the Catholic Encyclopedia — and died on 22 May, dated 1153 by Wikipedia and Catholic Online but 1155 by the Catholic Encyclopedia. He wrote lives of St. John Gualbert and of St. Bernard of Vallombrosa, bishop of Parma, and in 1145 transferred relics of St. James of Compostella to Pistoia.
b.s: The works held here are his lives of St. John Gualbert, the founder of Vallombrosa, which present the order's origins (Itta's 1039 grant), its early holiness, its ferruginous habit, and Gualbert's virtue as a work of grace against simoniacs.

w: Book on the Fountain of Life
Excerpts from the Book of Revelations

b.bio: Audradus Modicus, printed here as Audradus of Sens, was a Frankish ecclesiastic and monk of Saint Martin's of Tours who served as auxiliary bishop (chorepiscopus) to Archbishop Wenilo of Sens from 847 until 849, when he was deposed by the Council of Paris along with the other Gallican chorepiscopi. He then went to Rome, where he presented his writings to Pope Leo IV. Hostile to Charles the Bald's brothers Lothair I and Louis the German, he wrote in verse and prose. The visions he claimed concerning the civil wars in France were committed to writing.
b.s: The works held here — a verse Liber de fonte vitae treating creation, the fall, grace, and last things; excerpts from his Liber revelationum; and his letter to Hincmar — show a Carolingian author combining exegesis with polemic, including argument directed against King Charles (the Bald) and the bishops assembled at Sens.

b.bio: A Roman monk of the monastery of St Andrew on the Caelian Hill, Augustine was sent by Pope Gregory I in 595 to lead the Gregorian mission to Kent. He landed in Thanet in 597, converted King Æthelberht, was consecrated bishop, and became the first Archbishop of Canterbury, establishing sees at London and Rochester by 604. His attempts to bring the native British bishops under his authority failed. The work held here, a privilege for Canterbury Abbey granting perpetual liberty and exemption from episcopal dominion, citing Gregory and Æthelberht's royal grant, is generally regarded as a later composition issued under his name rather than his own act.
b.s: As leader of the Gregorian mission he founded English Christianity and the see of Canterbury; the privilege preserved under his name documents early claims of monastic immunity against archiepiscopal and secular control.

b.bio: No surviving record gives dates, offices, or biography for an Augustinus Fortunius, so none are asserted here. The reference works consulted all concern a different person of a similar name, Venantius Honorius Clementianus Fortunatus, sixth-century poet and bishop of Poitiers, and cannot be used to identify this author.
b.s: The single work held under this name is a six-page Third Life of Peter Damian (PL 144), a short hagiographical history defending Damian's hermit vocation and his charity, and polemicizing against the Milanese clergy faction, the counts of Tusculum, and imperial claims.

b.bio: Agostino Patrizi Piccolomini, born in Siena in 1436, was a priest, theologian, and bishop of Pienza who died in 1495 or 1496. He belonged to the Piccolomini family. Under commission from Pope Innocent VIII he revised the Roman Pontifical and wrote on papal ceremonial; his Ceremoniale Romanum was later passed off as his own work by Marcellus, archbishop of Corfu. Mabillon also printed from him a life of Fabianus Bentius and an account of Frederick III's reception by Paul II at Rome.
b.s: The library holds his epistle to Innocent VIII prefacing his ordered revision of the pontifical rites, arguing that ritual change preserves substance while accommodating times and that papal review guarantees liturgical authority against critics of its Latin.

b.bio: Antonio Agustín y Albanell, born in Zaragoza in February 1517 (sources differ on the day: Feb. 17 per Wikipedia and Catholic-Hierarchy, Feb. 26 per Encyclopedia.com), studied law at Bologna and became a doctor of laws there in 1541. Charles V appointed him auditor of the Roman Rota; Paul IV sent him as nuncio to England under Mary Tudor in 1555. He was bishop of Alife, then of Lérida (1561), and Gregory XIII made him archbishop of Tarragona in 1576. He took part in the Council of Trent's reforms. His scholarship centered on Roman and canon law; his De emendatione Gratiani is a critical examination of the text of Gratian's Decretum.
b.s: The notes held here belong to his critical work on Gratian's Decretum: they correct misattributed canons (e.g., a chapter falsely inscribed from Carthage IV), trace communion-suspension rules to apostolic canon 74, and argue that causes are judged by provincial synods with appeal to provincial or universal councils.

b.bio: Aunarius (Aunacharius), a noble from the Orléans region, was raised at the Burgundian royal court, instructed and ordained by Syagrius of Autun, and became Bishop of Auxerre. He enforced daily attendance at the Divine Office, organized rotating litanies, held a diocesan synod whose 45 canons treat marriage and popular superstition, attended the councils of Paris (573) and Mâcon (581/583/585), received letters from Pope Pelagius II urging Frankish aid against the Lombards, and caused lives of his predecessors Amator and Germanus to be written.
b.s: The single page held here is an epistle asserting that saints' lives should be written in both verse and prose — consistent with his known concern for the cult of saints and his commissioning of vitae of Amator and Germanus.

b.bio: Aurelian of Réôme (Aurelianus Reomensis) was a Frankish monk and music theorist of the mid-ninth century. He was a member of the monastery of Saint Jean de Réôme in the Côte-d'Or but says he was dismissed from the community for an unspecified offense. He wrote his treatise as penance, at the request of colleagues, to supplicate Abbot Bernard, who is recorded there from 846 and soon after became bishop of Autun; this fixes the work's date. An identification with Aurelian, archbishop of Lyon (876–895), rests on circumstantial evidence only.
b.s: His Musica disciplina is the earliest extant medieval European treatise on music and contains the earliest information on the melodic character of the church modes; the letter held here is its dedicatory preface to Bernard, pleading forgiveness while surveying prayer, grace, angels, and the power of music over affections.

b.bio: Aurelius was bishop of Carthage from about 391 until his death around 429 or 430; the Catholic Encyclopedia dates his episcopate 388–423. He was a friend and patron of Augustine of Hippo, funding the monastic community at Hippo that served as a training ground for bishops. As bishop he convoked and presided over the plenary councils of Africa held almost yearly, signed synodal letters in the name of all participants, and led the African church through its two great crises: the last Donatist resurgence and the first appearance of Pelagianism. He was among the first bishops to denounce Pelagianism, excommunicated Celestius from Carthage in 412, and condemned Pelagius and Celestius in a synod in 416; he also presided over the Council of 419 that codified 'The Code of Canons of the African Church'.
b.s: The works held here are his epistles and synodal letters condemning Pelagius and Coelestius as heretics justly condemned, upholding the Carthaginian synod's condemnation of the Donatists, asserting that all bishops must subscribe to the condemnation, and defending the preservation of the apostolic see's decrees and records.

w: Act of Thanksgiving to the Emperor
Commemoration of the professors of Bordeaux
Summaries of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey

b.bio: Decimus Magnus Ausonius was born around 310 at Burdigala (Bordeaux), son of a physician, and educated there and at Toulouse under his uncle Arborius. He taught grammar and then rhetoric at Bordeaux until Valentinian I summoned him to Trier to tutor Gratian, who later made him prefect of Gaul and consul in 379. After Gratian's murder in 383 he retired to his estates on the Garonne and wrote poetry. The library holds sixteen of his works from PL 19: Idylls, Letters, Epigrams, the Commemoration of the professors of Bordeaux, Parentalia, Ephemeris, and other occasional pieces.
b.s: His works here are occasional verse — letters, epigrams, epitaphs, and commemorations — that document the schools, families, and Christianizing elite of fourth-century Gaul; the record shows him arguing against Paulinus and citing Virgil (Maro) and Homer most often.

b.bio:
Ausonius of Bordeaux (c. 310–c. 395) — Decimus Magnus Ausonius was born around 310 at Burdigala (Bordeaux), son of a physician, and educated there and at Toulouse under his uncle Arborius. He taught grammar and then rhetoric at Bordeaux until Valentinian I summoned him to Trier to tutor Gratian, who later made him prefect of Gaul and consul in 379. After Gratian's murder in 383 he retired to his estates on the Garonne and wrote poetry. The library holds sixteen of his works from PL 19: Idylls, Letters, Epigrams, the Commemoration of the professors of Bordeaux, Parentalia, Ephemeris, and other occasional pieces.

Theodosius I (c. 347–c. 346) — Flavius Theodosius, born at Cauca in Gallaecia (Spain) on 11 January 347 (older authorities give c. 346), son of the general Comes Theodosius. After service against the Sarmatians as Dux of Moesia and a period of retirement following his father's execution (376), Gratian named him Augustus for the East on 19 January 379 after Valens died at Adrianople. He ruled the East from 379 to 392 and was sole emperor from 392 until his death at Milan on 17 January 395, succeeded by Arcadius and Honorius. He established the Nicene Creed as the norm of orthodoxy and convened the Council of Constantinople (381).
b.s: His works here are occasional verse — letters, epigrams, epitaphs, and commemorations — that document the schools, families, and Christianizing elite of fourth-century Gaul; the record shows him arguing against Paulinus and citing Virgil (Maro) and Homer most often.

b.bio: Auspicius of Toul (Auspicius Tullensis) was a fifth-century bishop of Toul, the fifth recorded in that see, and a saint of the Roman Catholic church. Sources disagree on his death date: one gives about 490, two older cyclopedias give 474. He belonged to the Gallo-Roman aristocracy and counted the general Arbogast among his ancestors; he succeeded Gelsimus around 478 and was thus the first bishop of Toul to serve under Frankish rule. He was a friend and correspondent of Sidonius Apollinaris and of Count Arbogast of Trier, and wrote iambic verse based on stress rather than classical quantity.
b.s: The library holds his verse Epistle to Arbogast, a letter of moral instruction arguing that cupidity is the root of all evils, that Christian faith surpasses pagan virtue, and that almsgiving extinguishes cupidity's poison. The library record shows it argues against the ancient (pagan) Arbogastes and cites Scripture alongside Iamblichus.

w: Charter of the monastery of Wallers

b.bio: Aubert (Autbert) was consecrated bishop of the united sees of Arras and Cambrai on 24 March 633, succeeding Aldebert. He promoted religion and monasticism in Hainaut and Flanders, built churches and abbeys including Hautmont (652), and figures such as Landelin, Ghislain, Waltrude, and Aldegundis passed through his hands. The library holds under his name only a one-page charter concerning the monastery of Wallers from PL 80, so his presence here rests on that document rather than on any treatise.
b.s: The single item held is an administrative charter for the monastery of Wallers, evidence of episcopal patronage of Merovingian monasticism rather than theological writing.

b.bio: Avesgot (Avesgaud) was a monk and then abbot of the monastery of La Couture, in a suburb of Le Mans, from after 1061 until 1079, when Johel succeeded him. He must not be confused with Avesgaud de Bellême, bishop of Le Mans who died c. 1035/36, nor with another Avesgaud, abbot of Saint-Vincent at Le Mans, present at Philip I's coronation in 1039; sources note he may have come from the same Bellême house as both. He describes his family as powerful in the Maine.
b.s: The library holds his single surviving work, an epistle to Anselm of Canterbury written while Anselm was still at Bec, citing Lanfranc and Guimond; it shows learned correspondence between Norman monastic circles before Anselm's rise.

b.bio: The library prints this name as 'Avitus the Priest,' and the work held here decides who he is: not Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus, bishop of Vienne (c. 450–c. 519), whom The surviving records describe, but a different namesake. He was a priest who wrote an account of the discovery and translation of the relics of St. Stephen, addressed to a correspondent named Palchonius, preserved in Migne's Latin patrology (PL 41).
b.s: His Letter to Palchonius treats the inventio of St. Stephen's relics, arguing that written testimony guarantees relic authenticity and that the relics of martyrs aid the faithful as patrons.

b.bio: Avitus (c. 450–519) — Alcimus Ecdicius Avitus, born c. 450 into a Gallo-Roman senatorial family related to the emperor Avitus, succeeded his father Hesychius as bishop of Vienne around 490. As metropolitan he led a public conference between Catholic and Arian bishops held before King Gundobad at Sardiniacum near Lyon in 499, and later won the conversion of Gundobad's son Sigismund to Catholicism. He also opposed Semipelagianism and defended Roman primacy in correspondence with Pope Hormisdas during the Acacian schism.
b.s: The work held here is his record of that episcopal conference: a disputation in which Avitus defends the consubstantial Trinity against an Arian king's objections, arguing that abandonment of God's law brings national ruin while peace with God yields political peace.

w: Election of St. Maiolus as Abbot of Cluny

b.bio: Aymard was a Benedictine monk of Cluny, elected third abbot in 942 after Odo's death when the prior Hildebrand declined the office. He continued the Cluniac reform and attended closely to the abbey's material administration: its property expanded considerably through donations from the wealthy and powerful during his abbacy. In 948 Pope Agapetus II confirmed Cluny's direct dependence on the Apostolic See. Having gone blind, he resigned in 948 after arranging Mayeul's election as successor, then lived as a simple monk until his death at Cluny on 5 October 965.
b.s: The two items held here are not treatises but records from his abbacy preserved in PL 137: a cartulary of royal and noble grants to Cluny and an account of St. Maiolus's election, documenting how royal confirmation secured the abbey's property and its dependence on Rome.

b.bio: Adrien Baillet was a French priest and critic born at Neuville en Hez near Beauvais. Educated at the College of Beauvais and ordained priest in 1676, he served briefly as curate of Lardieu and canon of Beaumont before becoming librarian to the advocate-general de Lamoignon in Paris, where he compiled an analytical catalogue of that library. He wrote prolifically as an erudite, historian, and religious author, including the Jugements des savans sur les principaux ouvrages des auteurs and a biography of Descartes, and worked on a large Lives of the Saints.
b.s: The two pages held here are Baillet's introductory notice on Victor of Utica printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 58, where he surveys the evidence for Victor's exile in Africa under the Vandal king Thrasamund, notes that Guntamund later slackened the Arian persecution, and defends the thesis that forbidding episcopal succession destroys the church and that bishops must ordain despite royal prohibition.

b.bio: Antoine Beaugendre was a French Benedictine of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, entering it in 1646, and served as librarian of the abbey of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; he was born in Paris around 1628. His principal scholarly work was a new edition with notes of the works of Hildebert (bishop of Mans and archbishop of Tours) and Marbod (bishop of Rennes), printed at Paris in 1708; he also wrote a life of Messire Joly, canon and founder of the Hospitaller sisters at Dijon. He died on August 16, 1708.
b.s: The works held here are his prefatory material and an epistle from PL 171 — front matter to his 1708 edition of Hildebert and Marbod — arguing that both bishops belong among Gallican saints and defending Hildebert's voluntary abdication of his bishopric for the contemplative life.

b.bio: The name covers at least two distinct men whom the sources do not reconcile with what this library holds. One Antonio Caracciolo, a Theatine cleric regular (c.1560-1642), wrote on Neapolitan church history and the cult of St Januarius (PRDL; McClintock & Strong); another, born c.1515 into the Melfi family, became bishop of Troyes and died in 1569 (Treccani; Wikidata/Catholic Hierarchy). Neither source connects either man to a preface printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 173, so the author of the single item held here cannot be identified with confidence from these records.
b.s: The library holds only a preface from PL 173 under this name; readers should not assume it belongs to either the Theatine historian or the sixteenth-century bishop of Troyes without further evidence.

b.bio: Antonio Carafa was born in Naples on 25 March 1538 to Rinaldo I Carafello Carafa and Giovanna of the signori of Montefalcone, a relative of Pope Paul IV through whose household he entered the Roman Curia in 1555. He studied at Padua and Naples, became a canon of the Vatican basilica in 1558, was expelled from Rome in 1561 during the trials of the Carafa family, and was reappointed to his canonry on 1 June 1566 after Pius V rehabilitated the family. Created cardinal deacon on 24 March 1568 by Pius V, he served as Prefect of the Tribunal of the Apostolic Signature from 29 January 1569 until his death in Rome on 13 January 1591, was appointed protector of the Maronites on 9 December 1569 (sending missions to Lebanon in 1578 and 1580), sat on Gregory XIII's 'congregation of the Greeks' created in 1573, and succeeded Guglielmo Sirleto as Librarian of the Holy Roman Church (1585–1591). He also presided over the Vulgate commission under Sixtus V.
b.s: The library holds only an index of titles from PL 77 under his name; his standing rests on his Latin translations of Greek patristic texts — notably Theodoret's Psalms commentary and Gregory of Nazianzus' Orationes — and his direction of the Sixtine Vulgate edition.

b.bio: The name printed here does not match the person the sources describe: André Duchesne (May 1584 – 30 May 1640) was a French historiographer to the king under Richelieu, born at L'Île-Bouchard, known for genealogies and critical collections of French history. Nothing in those sources connects him to the two Latin pieces held here, which belong to the ninth-century dispute over Ebbo of Reims. The works themselves are the only evidence for who wrote them, and they give no name beyond the attribution on the shelf.
b.s: The two pieces here are documents of the Ebbo of Reims controversy: they argue that Ebbo's forced resignation under persecution was no true desertion, that his canonical election by clergy and people made him bishop, that ordinations by a legitimately restored bishop are valid, and that restitution required the apostolic see's authority — all directed against Hincmar of Reims.

b.bio: The 'Anonymous Clergy of Ravenna' refers to the collective ecclesiastical body or an unnamed representative of the clergy of Ravenna during the early ninth century. Under the reign of Charlemagne, this group addressed formal correspondence to his son, Charles the Younger, King of the Franks. The letter reflects the local clergy's engagement with Carolingian political authority and ecclesiastical administration in northern Italy following the integration of the Exarchate of Ravenna into the Frankish sphere.
b.s: Their surviving epistle provides valuable historical and theological evidence for the administrative and ecclesiastical relations between northern Italian sees and the Carolingian dynasty.

b.bio: The library prints this name over a single six-page 'Admonition' in PL 17, but no source identifies an author so called; nothing can be asserted about this author's life.
b.s: The work held under this name is a brief admonitory piece printed among patristic texts in Migne's PL 17; its actual authorship remains unestablished by surviving records.

b.bio: Dinooth (Dinothus, Dunawd), first abbot of Bangor Iscoed, was originally a North British chieftain who took up religious life under Cyngen, prince of Powys, and founded Bangor on the Dee with his sons Deiniol, Cynwyl, and Gwarthan. Rees places him between 500 and 542; Bede names him as abbot at the second conference at Augustine's Oak (Hist. Eccl. ii.2), though only cautiously ('Tempore illo Dinoot abbas praefuisse narratur') and without authority, so the chronology placing him alive around 602–603 is uncertain. The work held here cannot be his own composition: it cites Spelmannus, a seventeenth-century antiquary, so it is a later text circulated under his name.
b.s: The library's single item, a 'Response to Augustine the Monk,' uses Dinooth's name to argue that the British church was not subject to Rome—that the archbishop of Caerleon was its metropolitan—and that it used eastern rather than Roman rites, citing the Council of Ephesus as sanctioning such autocephalous churches against patriarchal claims.

b.bio: The library prints this author as 'Ecclesia Africana', a collective attribution rather than a named person. The one work held is an epistle printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina volume 87 which defends the judgment and confirming authority of the apostolic see at Rome, requires ecclesiastical causes to be referred thither, and attacks the doctrinal novelties of Paul of Constantinople and Pyrrhus. None of The surviving records describes this epistle or its date; they concern other subjects.
b.s: The held epistle is a polemical petition asserting Roman primacy and the expulsion of novelty from the churches, directed against Paul of Constantinople and Pyrrhus.

b.bio: This entry covers a collective authorship: the short letter on Leporius printed among the works of Augustine (PL 31) is addressed in the name of several African bishops rather than one man. The letter concerns Leporius, a monk who had written against the Trinity and then submitted to correction. Its argument is pastoral as much as doctrinal: the fallen brother is to be restored with gentleness, since one God works through both condemning and healing ministers. None of the surviving records concerns the signatories of this letter — they describe other individuals (Possidius of Calama, Cyprian of Carthage, Fulgentius of Ruspe, and a modern Ugandan bishop) — so no names, dates, or sees are asserted here.
b.s: The single work held here is an early-fifth-century African episcopal letter showing how conciliar collegial correction was practiced toward a repentant heterodox monk.

w: On the Affairs of the Church of Rochester

b.bio: Ernulf, printed here as Arnulf of Rochester, was born at Beauvais around 1040 and studied under Lanfranc at Bec. He joined the monks of Christ Church, Canterbury after 1070, was made prior by Archbishop Anselm in 1096, became abbot of Peterborough in 1107, and bishop of Rochester in 1114; he died on 15 March 1124. Trained also under Ivo of Chartres, he was regarded as an expert in canon law. The two works held under his name fit this man: a letter on incestuous marriages citing Lanfranc and King William, and a history of the affairs of the church of Rochester.
b.s: The works held here show a canonist applying patristic authority and conciliar decrees to marriage law — upholding the binding force of ecclesiastical custom, allowing separation of spouses for adultery (the innocent party may dismiss the guilty for fornication), and defending the councils' decree of perpetual abstinence as penance for incest against preachers of the divine word who permitted such divorces.

b.bio: No source in hand identifies an 'Antonio Espinosa' matching the work held here — a prefatory address defending a Martin whose doctrine was drawn from Gregory, Isidore, and Peter Lombard, and citing Lucas of Tuy and Franciscus Antonius, archbishop of Toledo. The biographical surviving records instead describe Antonio Vázquez de Espinosa (d. 1630), a Carmelite friar, missionary and chronicler of Spanish America, author of the Compendio y descripción de las Indias Occidentales; his career and writings do not match this record, so nothing from them is asserted here.
b.s: The single piece held under this name is an editor's or compiler's address to the reader arguing that the works of Martin accord with Catholic faith and that preaching requires truth rather than eloquence.

b.bio: Andrea Gallandi, born at Venice on 7 December 1709 and died there in January 1779 (some sources give 1780), was an Italian Oratorian priest and patristic scholar. He pursued theological and historical studies under the Dominicans Daniello Concina and Bernardo de Rossi (de Rubeis), keeping up friendships with both after joining the Oratory of St. Philip Neri. His reputation rests on the Bibliotheca veterum patrum antiquorumque scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Graeco-Latina (Venice, 1765–81, 14 vols.), a collection of 380 ecclesiastical writers of the first seven centuries that gathered smaller and less accessible writings with Greek texts, Latin translations, and notes. He also published De vetustis canonum collectionibus dissertationum sylloge (Venice, 1778), assembling treatises of famous canonists such as Coustant and the Ballerini.
b.s: The works held here are his editorial apparatus — notices, prolegomena, and dissertations prefixed to patristic texts in the Migne series — in which he weighs questions of authenticity, dating, and textual recension for authors ranging from the Clementines (PG 2) to Saint Patrick (PL 53).

w: Historical and literary notice on St. Valerian

b.bio:
Galland, André (c. 1709–1780) — Andrea Gallandi (Gallandius), born at Venice 7 December 1709 and died there in January 1779 or 1780, was an Italian Oratorian priest and patristic scholar. He studied under the Dominicans Daniello Concina and Bernardo de Rossi before joining the Oratory of St. Philip Neri. His reputation rests on the Bibliotheca veterum patrum antiquorumque scriptorum ecclesiasticorum Graeco-Latina (Venice, 1765–81, 14 vols.), a collection of 380 writers of the first seven centuries favoring smaller and less-known works with Greek texts, Latin translations, and critical notes. He also compiled De vetustis canonum collectionibus dissertationum sylloge (Venice, 1778) and left an unpublished Thesaurus antiquitatis ecclesiasticae.

Schoenemann, Friedrich G. (unknown) — No surviving record identifies this Friedrich G. Schoenemann. The sources at hand describe other men of similar names — Karl Traugott Gottlieb Schönemann (1766–1802), a Göttingen jurist and editor of patristic letters, and Friedrich Schönemann (1886–1956), a German Americanist, university teacher, and politician — but neither can be attached to an author contributing a notice to Migne's Patrologia Latina. What is known is only what the library record shows: a four-page historical and literary notice on St. Valerian printed in PL 52.
b.s: Readers meet him here as the learned prolegomenist whose historical-literary notice on Valerian defends that author's orthodoxy against his accusers and weighs Sirmond's stylistic attribution of the homilies.

b.bio: The library holds one work under this name (PL 96), an embassy addressed to the Lombard king Aistulf urging him to restore the exarchate and submit to the Church. the surviving records describe two other men named Garnier who cannot be this author: Garnier de Rochefort (died c. 1225), abbot of Clairvaux and bishop of Langres, and Jean Garnier (1612–1681), the Jesuit patristic editor. Neither lived in the mid-eighth century when Aistulf reigned, so neither identification is adopted here.
b.s: The work preserved here is a diplomatic-theological address to Aistulf, arguing that peace outweighs victory, that justice rather than extent of provinces is true greatness of kings, that unjustly gained dominion is unstable like Nebuchadnezzar's statue, and that princely submission to the Church is glorious.

b.bio: Alard Gazet (Latinized Alardus Gazaeus), born 1 October 1566 and died 26 September 1626, was a French philologist and priest at the royal abbey of Saint-Waast in Arras. He should not be confused with his near-contemporary Guillaume Gazet (1554–1612), poet and ecclesiastical historian of Arras, whose works are separate. The works held under this name are Gazet's prefatory and excerpted commentary material from his edition of John Cassian's complete works, reprinted by Migne in Patrologia Latina volumes 49 and 58. In them he treats Cassian's life — Scythian birth, conversion under Chrysostom, monastic profession at Bethlehem, ordination as deacon by Chrysostom — and defends Cassian against charges of Pelagianism, arguing against Prosper of Reggio, Baronius, Honorius of Autun, and Origenist opponents.
b.s: Gazet matters here as the editor whose biographical and apologetic commentary frames the library's texts of John Cassian; the works held are his preface and excerpts defending Cassian against Pelagian and anti-Cassian critics.

w: Verses for the Tomb of St. Remigius

b.bio: The library prints 'Abbot Halduin', which corresponds to Hilduin, Abbot of Saint-Denis. The sources disagree on his dates: Wikipedia gives c. 785 to c. 855, while the Catholic Encyclopedia gives death on 22 November 840. He came from a prominent Frankish family, was educated under Alcuin or possibly Waldo of Reichenau, became abbot of Saint-Denis in 814/815 with further abbeys added, served Louis the Pious as archchaplain from about 819 or 822, joined Lothair's Roman expedition of 824, sided with Louis's sons in the war of 830, was banished to Paderborn and Corvey, and was later reinstated at Saint-Denis. Hincmar of Reims was among his pupils.
b.s: The single work held here is a one-page set of verses for the tomb of St. Remigius in PL 129, a minor piece by a major Carolingian administrator and scholar.

b.bio: Two different men appear under this name in the sources, and neither can be tied with certainty to the piece held here. One is Alphons Hueber, a Benedictine of Tegernsee in Upper Bavaria, born 1668 in Austria, entered the order 1688, professor at Freising from 1698, pastor at Egern (1705) and Pfarrvikar at Loiben (1720), died 12 January 1734; his listed writings are German devotional works. The other is Alphons Huber (1834–1898), an Austrian historian, lecturer then professor at Innsbruck and later professor at Vienna. The library's item, a prefatory 'To the reader' in PL 139 arguing that Gustavus Selenus's book treats chess only and not rhythmomachia, matches neither man's attested works.
b.s: The single work held here is a prefatory note distinguishing rhythmomachia from chess as treated by Gustavus Selenus, citing Gerbert, Fabricius, Buxerius, Barrozzi, Faber Stapulensis, and Thomas Topcliffus.

b.bio: René-Ambroise Janvier was born at Sainte-Osmane in 1613 and died in Paris on 25 April 1682. He made profession at the abbey of Vendôme in 1637 and belonged to the Congregation of Saint-Maur, where he became one of the congregation's leading Hebrew scholars, teaching Hebrew for years at Vendôme and elsewhere before moving to Saint-Germain-des-Prés. His chief publication is a Latin translation of David Kimhi's commentary on the Psalms (Paris, 1666); he also published an elegy in Hebrew verse on Jérôme Bignon (1656). The Library of Congress dates his birth 1614; French sources give 1613.
b.s: The two pieces held here — a preface and dedicatory letter in PL 202 — treat the Church and true worship, citing Jacques Sirmond, Alexander III, Alberic the Roman chancellor, and addressing the Senate of the Gallican Clergy.

b.bio: Leduin was abbot of the royal abbey of Saint-Vaast at Arras from about 1020 to about 1040, succeeding Richard of Verdun, whose restoration he continued by adopting the Cluniac observance and rebuilding the abbey church. A charter of 13 January 1024, issued at Rouen and attested by Duke Richard II, records an exchange between Saint-Vaast and Jumièges (Haspres for Angicourt) in his name: 'Ego Leduinus abbas.' The work held here is a one-page constitutional notice on the abbey's court, citing Leduinus himself and Count Baldwin (the Fair-Beard), and fixing rules on pleading, head-tax, advocacy, marriage across laws, mortmain, and alienation of allodial land.
b.s: He led Saint-Vaast's adoption of the Cluniac reform in early eleventh-century Flanders, and the record here preserves a charter-like constitution governing the abbey's public plea and its men's exemptions.

w: Authors and books in the Decree of Anselm
Authors and books in this canonical collection

b.bio: Angelo Mai (Angelus Maius), born at Schilpario in the diocese of Bergamo on 7 March 1782 and died in September 1854, was a Jesuit-trained philologist who made his name recovering lost texts from palimpsests using chemical reagents. He worked first at the Ambrosian Library in Milan from 1811, then moved to the Vatican Library at the end of 1819, where he discovered Cicero's De re publica among other texts. He became a cardinal in 1837 and served as archivist of the Holy See from 1853 until his death in 1854. The pieces held here under his name are editorial matter: prefaces, admonitions, historical notices, and surveys of authors and books prefixed to Migne's Patrologia Latina volumes.
b.s: The works here are Mai's editorial apparatus for the Patrologia Latina — prefaces, admonitions, and notices identifying authors, manuscripts, and contents of volumes such as those of Sicard of Cremona's Mitrale and canonical collections — so the reader should treat them as guides to the texts that follow, not as theological works in their own right.

w: Diatribes Illustrating the Deeds of Liberius and Damasus

b.bio: Antonius Merenda is known here as the author of diatribes on Pope Liberius and the Sirmium creeds, printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina 13. None of the sources consulted gives his dates, birthplace, or offices; the name variants recorded by Biblissima include Titus Antonius Merenda and Tito Antonio Merenda. Two ancient Romans named Antonius Merenda appear in reference works — a decemvir of 450–449 BC and his son, a consular tribune of 422 BC — but these are unrelated to this author and are disregarded.
b.s: His diatribes defend Liberius: they argue that Liberius in exile accepted the first Sirmium formula against Photinus, that only the second Sirmium formula was heretical, that the letter of Liberius to the Orientals is genuine, and that Demophilus was a perpetual semi-Arian — disputing Tillemont and other critics.

w: Notes on the Form of Institution of Canons

b.bio: Aubert Miraeus (Latinized Aubertus Miraeus, also called Aubert le Mire) was born in Brussels on 30 November 1573 and died at Antwerp on 19 October 1640. After studying at Douai and Leuven, he became canon of Antwerp cathedral in 1608 and secretary to his uncle Joannes Miraeus, Bishop of Antwerp. In 1611 Archduke Albert appointed him almoner and librarian; in 1624 he became dean of Antwerp cathedral and vicar general of the diocese. He wrote some thirty-nine works on profane, ecclesiastical, and monastic history; the Catholic Encyclopedia judges him reliable overall though some works lack thoroughness and accuracy.
b.s: The library holds only six pages under his name: notes arguing that the Aachen canons were secular clergy rather than Augustinian regulars, that their rule was drawn from many fathers rather than Augustine alone, and correcting misattributions (including assigning De officiis to Amalarius of Metz).

w: Scholia on all the works of Saint Eulogius
Scholia on the Life of Saint Eulogius

b.bio: Born at Cordoba in 1513 and died there in 1591, Morales studied at Salamanca and Alcalá, took Holy orders, and was elected to the chair of Belles-Lettres at Alcalá. In 1574 Philip II appointed him chronicler of Castile to continue Florián de Ocampo's Crónica General de España, which he carried down to the union of Castile and León under Ferdinand I; his pupil Sandoval continued it down to 1079. His uncle was the humanist Fernán Pérez de Oliva. The works under his name here are his editorial apparatus on Eulogius of Córdoba: scholia on Eulogius's works and Life, excerpts, and an admonition.
b.s: The pieces held here are not free-standing treatises but Morales's learned commentary defending the ninth-century Cordoban martyrs — chiefly against their detractors, against Alvarus on points of chronology, and against Laurentius Surius — drawing on Pliny, Strabo, Ptolemy, Usuard, and Livy, and arguing that Spanish linguistic corruption dates from Gothic times and that Christians lived tolerated under Islamic law if silent about Muhammad.

b.bio: Two ninth- and tenth-century abbots named Odo appear in the sources: Odo of Cluny (born 878/879, died 18 November 942), second abbot of Cluny (927–942) and monastic reformer, whose attested writings are a life of Gerald of Aurillac, three books of Collationes, sermons, and the Occupatio; and Odo of Glanfeuil, ninth-century abbot of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés and hagiographer of St. Maurus (Life of St. Maurus, Miracula S. Mauri). Neither source attributes a Life of Saint Gregory to either man. The library holds one short hagiographical life under this name, heavy with miracle narratives, relic devotion, and citation of Fortunatus and St. Martin; its authorship cannot be assigned to either documented Odo on the evidence at hand.
b.s: The work here is a brief saint's life asserting that saints are rightly venerated for doctrine and example, that Christ is worshiped in the persons of the saints, and that relics carried on the body avert storms.

w: On the Life and Writings of Bonizo

b.bio: Andreas Felix von Oefele (Oefelius) was a Munich-born historian and librarian. After studies in law, history and theology at Ingolstadt and Leuven, he became a librarian at Leuven in 1727, then educator to the Bavarian princes Clemens and Max (sources place this appointment in 1734 or 1735). From 1746 until 1778 he headed the Electoral Court and State Library in Munich as 'Electoral Councillor, Bibliothecarius and Antiquarius', and he was among the founders of the Bavarian Academy of Sciences (1759). The sources differ on his death date: Wikipedia gives 17 February 1780, while the Bavarian State Library and JPortal give 24 February 1780.
b.s: The work held here is his critical dissertation on the life and writings of Bonizo of Sutri, arguing from internal evidence that Bonizo's Epitome predates Gregory VII's pontificate and reconstructing Bonizo's fall — capture by Henry IV — against Baronius, Ughellus, Ciaconius and Colettus.

b.bio: Alfonso (Alonso) Ortiz was a Castilian canon and chaplain to Queen Isabella, born at Villarrobledo (some sources say Toledo) and trained at Salamanca in Latin, Greek, Hebrew and Arabic, where he attained a doctorate cited in the Seville incunable of 1493. At the command of Cardinal Francisco Ximénez de Cisneros he revised and prepared for print the Mozarabic breviary and missal, published in the first years of the sixteenth century. He died shortly after 1503, when he left his library to the University of Salamanca. The two items held here under his name belong to that Mozarabic liturgical work: a table of Sundays and feasts and its dedication letter.
b.s: His works here are the paratexts of the restored Mozarabic rite printed under Cisneros, arguing that ancient liturgical offices deserve restoration and printing and identifying the Mozarabs as Christians living among the Arabs.

b.bio: Antoine Pagi, born at Rognes on 31 March 1624 and died at Aix-en-Provence on 5 June 1699, was a French ecclesiastical historian. After studying with the Jesuits at Aix he entered the Conventual Franciscans at Arles, making solemn profession on 31 January 1641, and was elected provincial, an office he held four times. He devoted his spare time to history, finding numerous chronological errors and misstatements in Baronius's Annales ecclesiastici and making their correction his life-work. His first volume appeared at Paris in 1689; the remaining three, reaching to 1198, were completed in manuscript before his death and edited by his nephew François Pagi (Geneva, 1705).
b.s: The works held here are his critical observations on Baronius's Annales: they assert that the synod of Onestrefelda was held in 701, that Bede accurately narrates the cause of Wilfrid of Northumbria, that the 704 synod read Agatho's acts only for Wilfrid's case, that the chapters attributed to Adrian I interpolate and alter the ancient canons, and that early papal epistles are supposititious forgeries — arguing chiefly against Baronius.

w: Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen

b.bio:
Abbot Paul (unknown) — Abbot Paul is known here as one of two authors named in the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen (PL 103), a monastic rule the text itself attributes to Paul and Stephen as its true authors and locates in Italy or Spain. The library's other item under this name, a short Rule for Monks (PL 66), treats the divine office, chant led by seniors with unanimous participation, psalm recitation for learners, and the prior's authority over departures from office and over tempo and pitch of singing. the surviving records describe two different men bearing the name Paul — Paul of Caen, Norman abbot of St Albans (d. 1093), and Paul the Deacon, the Lombard historian of Monte Cassino — neither of whom matches these works, so they are set aside.

Abbot Stephen (unknown) — The library holds under this name a short rule for monks, an epistle, and a rule ascribed to Saints Paul and Stephen. The works themselves argue that Paul and Stephen, abbots living in Italy or Spain, are the true authors of the rule, adducing Vulgate citations as evidence of pre-Jerome antiquity; their content orders subjection of juniors to seniors, permission from the prior before departing the divine office, chant begun by seniors and joined unanimously, psalm recitation for learners, and tempo and pitch governed by the prior's judgment. One text argues against Calmet.
b.s: The works held are monastic rules governing communal worship, chant, and obedience to superiors, attributed by their own text to Paul and Stephen as authors of pre-Jerome antiquity.

b.bio: Angelo Maria Quirini was born at Venice on 30 March 1680 and entered the Benedictine Order at Florence in the mid-1690s, later teaching Scripture there from 1705. After scholarly travels through Germany, the Netherlands, England and France (c. 1710–1714), he was named Bishop of Corfu in 1723, transferred to Brescia, created cardinal in 1726, and placed at the head of the Vatican Library in 1730; he later became prefect of the Congregation of the Index. He corresponded with Montfaucon, Newton and others, and edited patristic texts — the dedication letter held here belongs to that editorial work.
b.s: The single work here is his dedication letter to an edition of an ancient bishop's works, defending episcopal scholarship and the preservation of ancient monuments against critics, with Berengar of Tours cited as a cautionary example.

b.bio: Rainard (Raynald) of Bar, son of Count Milo II of Bar-sur-Seine, was a monk of Clairvaux and friend of Bernard of Clairvaux. He became the fifth abbot of Cîteaux around 1134, succeeding the deposed Guy, and led the order as it incorporated Obazine and Savigny in 1147. He took part in Bernard's reconciliation with Abelard and died at Provence during a visitation; he was buried at Cîteaux. He is credited with compiling the Instituta generalis capituli apud Cistercium, the earliest collection of Cistercian general chapter decisions, though one account holds that the collection was published not in 1134 but c. 1150–1151 by his successor Goswin.
b.s: The works held here are the Instituta Capituli Generalis Ordinis Cistercensis — statutes binding uniform observance of the Benedictine rule, identical liturgical books, plain clothing without furs, manual labor, and enclosure across all abbeys — and a letter to Pope Innocent II.

b.bio: The single item held under this name is a one-page Preface printed in volume 187 of Migne's Patrologia Latina. The biographical surviving records all concern Aemilius Ludwig Richter (1808–1864), a nineteenth-century German jurist and church-law professor at Leipzig, Marburg and Berlin; they do not identify or describe the writer of this Preface, and are therefore set aside as pertaining to a different person. Nothing in the sources or the library record establishes who wrote or signed this Preface.
b.s: The work held here is only a one-page Preface to PL 187; its authorship cannot be established from surviving records.

w: On the Translation of the Crucifix

b.bio: Angelus Maria Rivola is not identifiable with any of the better-known namesakes: Domenico Rivarola (1575–1627), Genoese cardinal; Angelo Maria Rivato (1924–2011), Jesuit bishop of Ponta de Pedras; or Angelo Mai, the nineteenth-century philologist. The work held here is a five-page account of the translation of a crucifix, transcribed from Vallombrosan acts and dedicated to Florentine prelates — Francesco Nerli, archbishop of Florence, and Filippo Soldani, bishop of Fiesole — and addressed to the grand duke of Tuscany under Pope Clement X. This places the author in late seventeenth-century Tuscany, but no source gives his dates, office, or biography.
b.s: His single held work is a short devotional history defending veneration of sacred images as an aid to devotion and contrition, arguing for uniformity of rite over variety.

b.bio: Angelo Rocca (Camers), born at Rocca Contrada near Ancona in 1545, entered the Augustinian convent of Camerino at age seven and took a doctorate in theology at Padua in 1577. He worked as an editor with Aldo Manuzio in Venice, then in Rome became secretary to the Augustinian superior general (1579), head of the Vatican Printing House and Secretary of the Congregation of the Index under Sixtus V (1585), papal sacristan (1595), and titular Bishop of Tagaste (1605). He helped produce the Clementine Vulgate and founded the Angelica Library in Rome. The scholia held here are his annotations on the liturgical treatise printed in PL 78.
b.s: The work here consists of scholia defending ancient liturgical usage — arguing that mass orations were called sacraments, that the canon's cross-signs represent the passion, and correcting translators and compilers such as Pamelius, Walafrid Strabo, and Gratian's text of Justinian.

b.bio: Andreas Schott, born in Antwerp on 12 September 1552 and died there 23 January 1629, was a Jesuit priest and philologist. He studied at the Collegium Trilingue of the University of Leuven under Cornelius Valerius and Theodoricus Langius, took theology under Michael Baius, and later taught rhetoric. He spent much of his career in Spain, including at the Colegio de Santa Catalina and the University of Zaragoza, before returning to Antwerp. He was chiefly an editor and translator of Latin and Greek classical literature. The two prefaces held here are his introductions to volumes in Migne's Patrologia Latina (PL 50 and PL 96).
b.s: The works here are his editorial prefaces to Migne's Patrologia Latina volumes, marking him as one of the scholarly editors whose apparatus shaped how seminarians read the Latin Fathers.

b.bio: Abraham Scultetus was born on 24 August 1566 in Grünberg, Silesia. Raised Lutheran, he studied at Wittenberg and Heidelberg and by 1595 was working for the Elector of the Palatinate; when exactly he became Reformed is unknown. He served as court preacher to Frederick V and became professor of Old Testament at Heidelberg in 1618. He was a prominent Palatine delegate at the Synod of Dort (1618–19), where he agreed with the condemnation of the Remonstrants. After the collapse of the Palatine cause he retired to Emden, where he died on 24 October 1625. The works held here are his Latin analyses of Lactantius printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina.
b.s: His analyses prefacing Lactantius's Divine Institutes and De ira Dei guide readers through Lactantius's case that both divine anger and favor must be attributed to God, against Epicurus, Lucretius, and the Stoics.

b.bio: The library holds under this name a short rule for monks, an epistle, and a rule ascribed to Saints Paul and Stephen. The works themselves argue that Paul and Stephen, abbots living in Italy or Spain, are the true authors of the rule, adducing Vulgate citations as evidence of pre-Jerome antiquity; their content orders subjection of juniors to seniors, permission from the prior before departing the divine office, chant begun by seniors and joined unanimously, psalm recitation for learners, and tempo and pitch governed by the prior's judgment. One text argues against Calmet.
b.s: The works matter chiefly as a disputed early monastic rule whose authorship and antiquity were contested, with the texts defending attribution to Paul and Stephen against Calmet.

w: Dissertation on the Collection of Canons
Dissertation on the Decree Attributed to Ivo

b.bio: Augustin Theiner, born at Breslau on 11 April 1804, son of a shoemaker, first studied theology, then law at Breslau and Halle, taking a law degree in 1829. A Prussian scholarship funded research in Belgium, England and France into the sources of canon law. Settling in Rome under Count Reisach's influence, he became a priest and entered the Oratory of St Philip Neri. Pius IX placed him in the Vatican Library in 1850 and made him Prefect of the Vatican Secret Archive in 1855. His history of Clement XIV, hostile to the Jesuits, was forbidden in the Papal States; late in life he breached official trust by retaining transcripts of the Council of Trent's acta against papal orders.
b.s: The works held here are not patristic texts but Theiner's critical dissertations and notices printed in Migne's Patrologia Latina, defending the attribution of the canonical collection to Anselm of Lucca, arguing it was made at Gregory VII's command, that its manuscripts contain interpolated documents drawn from similar contemporary collections, and that Parisian codices derive from Roman exemplars — against the Ballerini brothers, Gratian's Roman correctors, and other deniers of the attribution.

w: Critical Inquiry into the Compilation of Decrees

b.t: Roman Catholic historian of canon law
b.bio:
Theinerus, Augustinus (1804–1874) — Augustin Theiner, born in Breslau on 11 April 1804 to a shoemaker's family, first studied theology and then law at Breslau and Halle, taking a law degree at Halle in 1829. A Prussian scholarship funded research on the sources of canon law in Belgium, England, and France; he settled in Rome, was ordained, and joined the Oratory of St Philip Neri. In 1836 he published his Disquisitiones criticae on the sources of canon law. Pius IX placed him in the Vatican Library in 1850 and named him Prefect of the Vatican Secret Archive in 1855. His history of Clement XIV's pontificate, hostile to the Jesuits, was banned in the Papal States.

Laborans (c. 1120–1125 – 1189/1190) — Laborans de Pontormo was a native of Pontormo near Florence who studied in Paris and became a canon at Capua before 1160. Created cardinal deacon of S. Maria in Porticu by Alexander III in 1173, he later held the title of S. Maria in Trastevere (dated 1180 by the New Catholic Encyclopedia, 1182 by Wikipedia). Sources differ on his death date: Wikipedia gives c. 1189, the New Catholic Encyclopedia says most likely Rome around 1190. He belonged to the decretists, the school of canonists who commented on Gratian's Decretum. His Compilatio decretorum (also known as Codex Compilationis), finished in 1182 after some twenty years of work, rearranged Gratian's text into a more logical order with parts and capitularia, adding decretals and Lateran III canons.
b.s: The single work held here is a critical inquiry into the compilation of decrees of Laborans, arguing from the single surviving codex that Laborans divided his work into five books with parts and capitularia (plus a sixth book as an epilogue), that its chapters lack argument summaries unlike earlier collections, and that Laborans used only Gratian's Decretum as his source (Gratian writing under Eugenius III, Laborans by 1182); despite the 'Latin Fathers' shelf label, its author is a nineteenth-century scholar, not a patristic writer.

b.bio: Ursinus began as a monk at Saint-Maixent near Poitiers and later served as abbot of Saint-Martin at Ligugé, where he built a basilica that in 782 received the relics of Leodegar of Autun. He also commissioned the monk Defensor to compile the patristic florilegium Liber scintillarum. Later authors report that around 684 Bishop Ansoald of Poitiers asked Abbot Andulf's monks for a Life of Leodegar, martyred at Sarcing three years earlier, and that Andulf delegated the task to Ursinus; that original Life does not survive as such, though Bruno Krusch claimed to reconstruct it from Carolingian versions, an account Paul Fouracre came to accept by 1996. He is not Zacharias Ursinus, the sixteenth-century Reformed author of the Heidelberg Catechism.
b.s: The work held here is his Life (Passion) of St. Leodegar, a Merovingian martyr narrative defending the bishop against Ebroin and presenting episcopal election and clerical chastity as marks of holy office.

w: Notes on the Poem of Adalberon

b.bio: Adrien de Valois (Hadrianus Valesius), born in Paris on 14 January 1607 and educated at the Jesuit college of Clermont, was a French historian and Latin poet, brother of the patristic editor Henri Valois. He devoted himself to the history of France and its monuments, working from manuscript as well as printed records. His principal works were the Gesta Francorum (3 vols. folio; first volume 1646, remaining volumes 1658) and the Notitia Galliarum (1675), an alphabetical topographical lexicon of Gallic place names drawn from ancient authors and medieval chroniclers. He was named historiographe du roi in 1664. His son Charles published his critical remarks posthumously as Valesiana.
b.s: The work held here is his set of historical-critical notes on Adalbero of Laon's poem, where he dates the poem after Hugh Capet's death, argues Adalbero still lived past 1002, holds that Adalbero succeeded Rorico at Laon in 977 and that the poem was written by an aged Adalbero for Robert, and asserts that Adalbero treacherously betrayed Duke Charles to Hugh.

b.bio: Antoine d'Albon, of a Lyonnais noble family, was abbot of Savigny (from c. 1520) and later of Île Barbe (from c. 1525), served as lieutenant of the king in the government of Lyon, and held successively the sees of Arles and Lyon; he was consecrated bishop in 1564. Catholic-Hierarchy records him as Archbishop Emeritus of Lyon, born 1507 and died 24 September 1574, while French Wikipedia gives 1508 and death on 14 September 1573. A separate Father Antoine d'Albon, bishop-elect of Arras around 1500, is a different man and not this author.
b.s: The library holds only his three-page dedication and preface in PL 21, in which he frames the patristic volume with a strongly Roman polemic: the Roman see as pillar and foundation of truth, Gallican fidelity to Rome as the church's safeguard, and Trent as moral and doctrinal reform.

b.bio: Two Frenchmen bore this name, and the sources do not settle which stands behind the work held here. Antoine Vyon d'Hérouval (Fort de Meulan 1606 – Paris 1689) was a diplomatist and antiquary, auditor at the Chambre des comptes (resigned his office in 1670), who searched monastic libraries for unpublished charters and collaborated with Luc d'Achery, the Maurist editor whose collections fed Migne's Patrologia Latina. His son Antoine-Paul Vyon d'Hérouval (Paris 1645 – Paris 1719) entered the canons regular of Saint-Victor, took his doctorate at the Sorbonne on 17 February 1673, served as librarian of Saint-Victor, was classed among 'insignificant Jansenists' in a manuscript of July 1673, and appealed the bull Unigenitus on 18 October 1718. Given the father's work with d'Achery on patristic texts, the attribution to the elder Vyon is plausible but unconfirmed.
b.s: The library holds under this name only the Life of Saint Desiderius (PL 87, 13 pages), a hagiographical account treating conscience as a robust natural teacher, court life compatible with monastic virtue, meditation on hell against lust, priests' duty to learn scripture before teaching, earthly life as a contest for a heavenly crown, need for divine grace over the flesh, and grief for the dead kept within Christian measure.

b.bio: Alexander led the Church of Alexandria from about 313 until his death, succeeding Achillas. As a priest he had lived through the persecutions under Galerius and Maximinus. His patriarchate was dominated by three conflicts: the dating of Pascha, the schism of Meletius of Lycopolis, and above all the teaching of Arius, a presbyter who denied that the Son is God's own natural son. Alexander condemned Arius at a synod in Alexandria and carried the fight to the Council of Nicaea in 325, where he led the opposition to Arianism; he also mentored his successor Athanasius. Sources disagree on his death date: the Catholic Encyclopedia gives 17 April 326, while other records give 326 or 328.
b.s: His surviving letters — the encyclical letter after the Alexandrian synod and the letter to Constantinople — are the earliest anti-Arian documents and prepared the ground for Nicaea.

b.bio: Andrew of Crete, also called Andrew of Jerusalem, was born in Damascus around 650 to Christian parents and entered the Lavra (monastery) of Saint Sabbas near Jerusalem at fourteen. Sent as a representative of the Jerusalem Patriarchate to the Sixth Ecumenical Council (680–681), he later served as archdeacon at Hagia Sophia in Constantinople and became Archbishop of Crete during the reign of Justinian II. The year of his death is uncertain: sources give July 4, variously 712, 726, or 740. He was a homilist and hymnographer, best known for the Great Canon.
b.s: The volume held here (PG 97) collects his homilies: exegetical and festal preaching centered on Christology—Mary as Mother of God, the Word made containable in the womb, the cross as Christ's glory—with polemic against the Jews, Herod, Nestorians, Docetists, and Iconoclasts.
